titleEn: How ‘To Catch a Predator’ indulged America’s appetite for humiliation and punishment
titleZh: 【arts】How ‘To Catch a Predator’ indulged America’s appetite for humiliation and punishment
descriptionEn: The show presented itself as a crusade to protect children. But its appeal may have had as much to do with the pleasures of being able to play judge, jury and executioner from your living room couch.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
For a television show that was canceled nearly two decades ago, “ To Catch a Predator ” has been having quite a moment.

For years, the show entertained Americans by finding men seeking sex with minors in online chatrooms and luring them into decoy houses. The host, “Dateline NBC” correspondent Chris Hansen, would then confront the men on camera.

Now a fictional account of the show, “ Primetime ,” will arrive in movie theaters in late September 2026, starring Robert Pattinson as Hansen. It comes on the heels of “ Predators ,” a critically acclaimed 2025 documentary about the legacy of “To Catch a Predator.”

As scholars of American culture and criminology , we’ve researched and written about the popularity of “To Catch a Predator” and its spinoff programs “ Hansen vs. Predators ” and “ Takedown with Chris Hansen .” To us, these shows are part of a broader legacy of Americans’ cultural attachment to vigilantism : the belief that when the government fails to root out threats to society, ordinary people should step up and punish wrongdoers.

There was something about “To Catch a Predator” that took this genre of entertainment to new heights. Yes, there was the novelty of having the ultimate pariah – the pedophile – at its center. But there was also the ritual of humiliation and punishment that it celebrated, one that has since rippled across politics, social media and popular culture.

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, vigilantism was closely associated with anti-immigrant and anti-Black violence, most notoriously through lynching.

This kind of lethal vigilantism has declined dramatically. But popular culture has continued to offer Americans plenty of opportunities to fantasize about the thrills of taking the law into their own hands, whether through pulp novels like Mickey Spillane’s “Mike Hammer” series , comics like “ Batman ,” John Ford’s westerns or Showtime’s “ Dexter .”

As fear of violent crime grew over the course of the 1970s , a succession of popular films featured heroes who bypassed a supposedly ineffective legal system to defeat dangerous criminals.

In the 1971 film “ Dirty Harry ,” Clint Eastwood plays a police officer who goes rogue when a prosecutor refuses to bring a serial killer to justice because the incriminating evidence was illegally obtained. Using his trademark .44 Magnum revolver, Harry delivers justice for victims failed by the state. Three years later, “ Death Wish ” featured Charles Bronson starring as Paul Kersey, an architect who becomes a vigilante after his wife is murdered, and who goes on a killing spree of petty criminals as the police turn a blind eye.

As viewers cheered on fictional vigilantes finally “doing something” about crime, shrewd politicians harnessed their thirst for punishment. They campaigned on and passed “tough on crime” laws that packed the nation’s prisons. Government agencies increasingly enlisted the public’s vigilante impulse by encouraging neighborhood groups to surveil their communities , protect their homes with security systems and help the FBI by watching out for criminals at large on shows like “ America’s Most Wanted .”

When it premiered in 2004, “To Catch a Predator” tapped into a new fear: online stranger danger.

In the 1980s and early 1990s, statistically rare instances of strangers abducting white children from public spaces and murdering them became highly publicized . This helped fuel a moral panic about the vulnerability of children , particularly as mothers were increasingly working outside of the home .

The emergence of the internet generated a new kind of stranger danger: Now, online predators could reach through fiber-optic cables and groom children in their own homes.

No show did more to raise the alarm about this new form of stranger danger than “To Catch a Predator.” The show was originally a recurring segment on “ Dateline NBC ,” the weekly investigative television newsmagazine that had debuted in 1992.

In it, reporter Chris Hansen collaborated with a vigilante organization called Perverted Justice . The vigilantes posed as teenagers in online chat rooms, responded enthusiastically if adults oriented the conversation toward sex, and invited them to come to a suburban home. The unsuspecting targets who showed up instead found Hansen and a camera crew, who barged into the room on Hansen’s cue.

The segment proved so popular that NBC eventually gave Hansen his own show.

Free from any pretense of serious investigative journalism, “To Catch a Predator” became a form of “ humilitainment ” – programming that exposes and degrades deviant people for the pleasure of its audience. As crews surround the suspects with cameras they hold like weapons, panic washes over them as they are being publicly branded a sex offender. Indeed, the label of “child sex predator” is so toxic that these scenes amounted to a kind of social death.

By watching the scene through those cameras, viewers don’t just get to witness the punishment.

In some sense, they get to participate in it.

“Predators,” the documentary about the show, captures the dangerous consequences of merging crime control with humilitainment.

It details how, in 2006, the show tried – and failed – to lure a Texas prosecutor named William Conradt Jr. to its bait house. Producers subsequently pressured local police to attempt to arrest him. As the “Dateline” crew and police surrounded the house, Conradt died by suicide.

More recently, in a 2023 episode of the “To Catch a Predator” spinoff “Takedown,” Hansen netted an 18-year-old gay man in Michigan who thought he was meeting up with a 15-year-old boy. Michigan is one of a handful of states that does not grant an 18-year-old a general close-in-age exemption for attempting to have sex with a 15-year-old. This provision of the law eliminates or reduces criminal penalties for consensual sexual activity when the participants are close in age and one partner is below the legal age of consent.

A producer had urged Hansen not to air the segment, but he did anyway, destroying the young man’s reputation in his first year of adulthood. The documentary includes an interview with the young man’s mother while he can be heard sobbing off camera.

In our view, “Primetime” and “Predators” should not be understood as a sign that Americans are rethinking their embrace of vigilantism and humilitainment.

Amateur humiliation content has become widespread on the internet, giving Americans more opportunities than ever to indulge in gleeful disgust or righteous outrage. “Karen” and “ internet freakout ” videos expose people behaving rudely in public, while “ gym shaming ” videos mock poor workout form. Ring camera footage can capture homeowners confronting porch thieves or political canvassers .

For its part, “To Catch a Predator” lives on in everything from copycat sting shows to parodies , to Hansen-produced revivals. On platforms such as X and TikTok, videos made by Dads Against Predators circulate, often depicting violent assaults of men who showed up somewhere to meet a minor for sex.

The short videos rewrite the final moment of “To Catch a Predator,” in which Hansen calmly confronts and sternly chastises the would-be predator, before letting law enforcement take over.

Instead, the vigilantes in Dads Against Predators simply punch their targets in the face .

titleEn: Annie Dillard brought poetry into prose, pioneering a mystical form of creative nonfiction that critics both admired and misunderstood
titleZh: 【arts】Annie Dillard brought poetry into prose, pioneering a mystical form of creative nonfiction that critics both admired and misunderstood
descriptionEn: For Annie Dillard, the sonic intensity of poetry was critical to every form of writing she published throughout her life.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
Annie Dillard is rightly celebrated as a pioneer in creative nonfiction after her death on Sep. 15, 2026, at age 81 . But the dazzling, disorienting feel of Dillard’s work might be best understood as the often overlooked influence of poetry on her prose.

Dillard published her first full-length work of creative nonfiction, “ Pilgrim at Tinker Creek ,” when she was only 28. Winning her the 1975 Pulitzer Prize , this early book set the tone for her later work in creative nonfiction: the essay collection “ Teaching a Stone to Talk ,” and full-length works “ Holy the Firm ” and “ For the Time Being .” They all attend closely to the natural world, with a theologian’s eye and a poet’s idiom.

Dillard’s creative nonfiction about nature owes a debt to the lyrical prose of transcendentalists like Henry David Thoreau , whom Dillard cited as a major influence in her work. She was also overt about the central role that fiction played in her thinking in her book of literary criticism, “ Living by Fiction .”

But Dillard’s nonfiction, though undeniably prose, can have “ the shape and intensity of a poem ,” as her New York Times obituary puts it.

As a writer and writing professor , I think often about how blurred the boundary between poetry and prose really is. Annie Dillard’s work embodies this permeability.

Not all writing is the same. Prose typically features continuous sentences arranged in paragraphs. Poetry tends to be differentiated from prose by a deliberate organization of language that’s not determined by the page itself.

Prose poetry, the lyric essay and other hybrid forms of literature play at the intersection of genre , which usually defines these separate categories of writing. Creative nonfiction likewise aims to accurately convey reality while emphasizing literary style. The literary features of creative nonfiction are often drawn from fiction, with devices such as dialogue, scene and flashback.

But one of the distinctions of Annie Dillard’s nonfiction is how much her prose owes to poetry.

Poetry can be defined in many ways , but it tends to be characterized by honed, heightened language. Poems are often noted for their memorable images, rich sounds and foregrounding of emotion. Dillard’s nonfiction is shot through with images that arrest readers with their beauty or confront readers with their terror – as in her Harper’s essay “ The Death of a Moth ,” where the insect is drawn to a candle flame, becomes stuck in the wax and is transformed into a burning wick. In Dillard’s words:

“She burned for two hours without changing, without swaying or kneeling – only glowing within, like a building fire glimpsed through silhouetted walls, like a hollow saint, like a flame-faced virgin gone to God, while I read by her light, kindled, while Rimbaud in Paris burnt out his brain in a thousand poems, while night pooled wetly at my feet.”

It’s no accident that Dillard describes herself as reading the work of French poet Arthur Rimbaud by the light of the moth. She previously wrote that she loved how language sounds in French symbolist poetry , and Rimbaud was known to combine prose with his poetry in a way Dillard herself does.

In “ The Writing Life ,” Dillard describes the process of writing “a favorite, difficult book” – likely “Holy the Firm” – as akin to writing poetry. She notes that the writing was “so intense and accented, and the world it described was so charged with meaning,” that the idea of going further exhausted her.

To help her write, she read Conrad Aiken’s poetry aloud, describing it as “pure sound unencumbered by sense.” She would read a poetry anthology’s index of first lines because “the parallels sounded strong and suggestive.”

She also describes repeating a single line of Wallace Stevens’ poetry “for hours, like a song” while writing.

Dillard purposefully channeled poetry’s sonic density in her writing process; it comes as no surprise that the heightened register of these poems made its way into her prose.

Dillard’s virtuosic, visionary style isn’t for everyone. Writer Eudora Welty praised Dillard in her review of “Tinker Creek ,” but Welty also admitted “not (knowing) what she’s talking about” at times and that her writing “leaves something to be desired.” That something was what Welty called “straight narrative,” the clarity of “point, direction, and shape” more often demanded of prose than poetry.

The solitude of the narrator in Dillard’s nonfiction and her apparent disengagement with society also was a source of criticism. As critic William Deresiewicz put it, “There is no economy and no society ” in “Tinker Creek.” “We don’t know how Dillard lives, or how she makes a living, or much of anything about her circumstances.” Her mix of cultural disengagement and theological concern smacked to Deresiewicz of “hypocrisy and spiritual snobbery.”

In the contained world of lyric poetry, especially nature poetry, this hermetic perspective would be less of a fault. Her mystical encounters with the divine through the natural world are reminiscent of poets like Gerard Manley Hopkins , Wendell Berry and Mary Oliver . The narrow lens of her attention can be viewed as a poetic feature played out at length over her nonfiction essays and books.

Like an expressionist painting , poetry draws attention to how something is being depicted, not just what is being portrayed. Prose can do this, too – creative nonfiction, especially, and Annie Dillard’s writing most of all.

titleEn: The story of Little Italy’s Feast of San Gennaro is the story of how Italian immigrants became American
titleZh: 【arts】The story of Little Italy’s Feast of San Gennaro is the story of how Italian immigrants became American
descriptionEn: Italian immigrants used to be accused of clinging too tightly to the Old World. Today, millions gather in Little Italy to celebrate the food, faith and traditions they brought with them.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
For two weeks in September, everyone wants to be Italian – at least judging by the crowds at the annual Feast of San Gennaro in New York City’s Little Italy.

Founded in 1926, the largest and longest-running Italian festival in the United States celebrates its 100th anniversary this year, with locals and tourists alike descending upon Mulberry Street in Manhattan to celebrate Italian American culture.

To be sure, there’s plenty that’s commercialized: Frank Sinatra impersonators croon “New York, New York,” while vendors hawk shirts with quotes from “The Godfather” and “The Sopranos” at astronomical prices. Classic Italian American fare like chicken parm subs and sausage and peppers fly off food carts.

And yet in my work as a medievalist , I’ve explored how this festival champions traditions that go back thousands of years.

If anything, the fact that centuries-old rituals coexist with sweet Italian sausages and big, floppy pizza slices speaks to a lengthy, strenuous and beautiful process of cultural assimilation.

Between 1881 and 1920, over 4.5 million Italians immigrated to America. Thousands, most of whom hailed from southern Italy, settled on Manhattan’s Lower East Side to form what became Little Italy .

These “ huddled masses ” faced all sorts of difficulties: overcrowded tenements, trouble finding work, racial discrimination and suspicion of their southern Italian Catholic practices , particularly from Irish Catholics. The Italian procession of religious statues and the street parties that followed, the Irish argued, looked far too pagan and idolatrous to be considered “real” Catholicism. Irish suspicion of such practices were also shared by local Protestants.

But by the early 20th century, Italian communities had grown so large that they could fund their own Italian-speaking churches .

One such parish was the Church of the Most Precious Blood , built in 1904 on Baxter Street. In 1926, a group of parishioners led by Alexander Tisi organized a tribute to one of the most popular holy figures from southern Italy: St. Januarius, known in Italian as San Gennaro.

An early Christian bishop, Gennaro was brutally beheaded outside of Naples on Sept. 19 in AD 305 on account of his faith. His execution was one of several that took place during the Diocletian Persecutions , a systematic campaign against Christians by the Roman Empire.

Since then, southern Italians have attributed all sorts of miracles to his intercession, including extinguishing the volcanic fires of Mount Vesuvius in 1631.

He is also seen as something of a prophet. Since at least 1389 , two vials purportedly containing the saint’s blood have been venerated in Naples because of their inexplicable ability to liquefy on his feast days. The liquefaction has long been interpreted as a sign of the saint’s protection. On the other hand, Italians viewed the blood staying solid as the sign of a looming catastrophe. The Allied bombings of Naples in 1943 , for example, occurred after the blood failed to liquefy.

Since the later Middle Ages, Gennaro’s feast on Sept. 19 has been one of the most important dates on Naples’ calendar.

During medieval and Renaissance celebrations, pork was the meal of choice , with pigs often awarded to the winners of street games. Young men might wrestle a greased-up pig inside the Naples Cathedral, with the victor cooking the animal for supper.

Centuries of devotion transformed San Gennaro into a symbol of Neapolitan identity. New York’s festival was designed to preserve those traditions.

That first Feast of San Gennaro in 1926 gave Italian immigrants a rare opportunity to publicly profess the cultural identity they had left behind in Italy.

It began with a procession featuring a 3-foot statue of San Gennaro. Hoisted upon men’s shoulders, the saint traveled around the church and the surrounding streets. While en route, devotees tacked dollar bills to his body , as many still do today. There was no blood relic, but there was a purported bone fragment of Gennaro’s specifically donated for the occasion. The chip of bone was placed in a circular container called a reliquary and hung around the saint’s neck. Afterward, the Italians of Little Italy gathered around plates of roasted chicken to toast to their shared heritage and traditions.

The event was a big success. Just two years later, in 1928, The New York Times reported that thousands of ex-Neapolitans were congregating for a festival that had already extended from one day to a full week.

But with triumph came trouble. That same year, New York Police Commissioner Joseph Warren prohibited the procession, arguing that the dollar bills pinned to the statue represented the “ profanation of sacred religious symbols .” The decision was ultimately reversed by a New York Supreme Court judge, on the grounds that Warren violated the populace’s religious liberties.

Warren’s attempt to suppress the procession exemplifies the sort of religious prejudices plaguing Italian communities during that period. But it was not the only form of discrimination Italians faced.

The darkness of southern Italians’ skin subjected them to discrimination, birthing derogatory slurs like “guinea” or “swarthy.” The suspicion that Italian immigrants were prone to criminal behavior was reinforced by real mafia organizations , such as the infamous Black Hand.

These prejudices, combined with the establishment of Italian churches and feasts, led to the belief that Italian immigrants clung too strongly to the traditions of their homeland and refused to assimilate into American culture.

It was not until after World War II that outsiders no longer hesitated to participate in Italian culture and festivities.

In 1949 , local newspapers reported that thousands of people of various ethnic backgrounds attended the riotous feast, where they watched Italians dance to folk songs in the streets and symphonic bands parade through the neighborhood beneath a new innovation: colored string lights casting pops of green, white and red along the city streets. Food played a big role : Stalls piled high with fresh clams, pasta and pastries promised non-Italians an authentic taste of Italy.

From there, attendance ballooned. In the 1960s , chartered buses ushered in Italians from states as far away as Maine and Ohio. By the 1970s , the feast had some 3 million visitors a year. Many locals today still recall how, in the 1960s and 1970s, young men climbed greased-up steel poles set out in the street in hopes of claiming a cash prize. The oily affair was squashed over safety concerns in the 1980s.

Over the years, the feast has faced its own challenges from within the Italian community.

In 2007 , some inhabitants of Little Italy petitioned Mayor Michael Bloomberg to cancel the festival, citing the strain that tourists placed on the local neighborhood and mafia interference . In 1996, for example, 19 members of the Genovese crime family were arrested for gambling, collecting dues from vendors and even stealing money off Gennaro’s statue.

Nevertheless, Bloomberg declined to interfere. The event, he said , was a part of New York itself.

No one understands this more than the organizers of this year’s feast. When discussing the plans for 2026 , the committee declared that this event was not just an Italian festival, but a tribute to New York’s cultural melting pot.

The 100th festival is dedicated to the Italian Americans who contributed to the city’s birth, an honor that arrives at a moment of controversy. Two months prior, Mayor Zohran Mamdani omitted Little Italy from a map of the city’s immigrant enclaves, sparking immediate backlash . While Mamdani vowed to reinsert the neighborhood, some argued that the omission accurately reflected the dwindling number of Italians living along Mulberry Street.

The controversy underscores the question fueling the centenary: How should the immigrants who built the city of New York be honored, even as the descendants of many of those immigrants have left their old neighborhoods for different parts of the country?

Perhaps the answer is this year’s grand marshal, San Gennaro himself, who continues to serve as a bridge between the children of the Italian diaspora and their forefathers, just as he did in 1926.

titleEn: How libraries in Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and other Pennsylvania communities evolved from subscription clubs to vital public institutions
titleZh: 【arts】How libraries in Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and other Pennsylvania communities evolved from subscription clubs to vital public institutions
descriptionEn: The nation’s first successful circulating library was established almost 300 years ago by Benjamin Franklin in Philadelphia.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
As a librarian who researches and writes about library history in Pennsylvania , I was delighted to see the American Library Association’s efforts to celebrate its 150th anniversary this year, while making several mentions of Pennsylvania.

The ALA highlighted its 1876 founding in Philadelphia ; how Pittsburgh philanthropist Andrew Carnegie funded the construction of more than 1,600 library buildings throughout the United States; and Scranton’s Henry and Edith Carr , who attended and maintained records about the ALA’s early conferences for nearly 50 years.

But these stories just scratch the surface of how Pennsylvanians have contributed to American libraries and librarianship.

I published a book on Pennsylvania libraries from the 1700s through the 1940s , and I’m working on a sequel that extends the story to the early 2000s. Many scholars connect the beginning of public librarianship in the United States to ALA’s 1876 founding, but libraries’ roots go back much further .

The Library Company of Philadelphia , established in 1731 by Benjamin Franklin, was the nation’s first successful circulating library and was a model for many others.

These early “public” libraries – so called because they did not require users to affiliate with churches, colleges or other organizations – were run by stockholders who pooled funds to purchase books. The owners charged annual membership fees to others who wanted to join.

In the 19th century there was widespread desire among U.S. educators, women’s clubs, local government leaders and public-spirited citizens to provide libraries to everyone, whether or not they could afford to subscribe.

Today, some people incorrectly believe that steel magnate Carnegie was the first philanthropist to donate money for library buildings. However, a number of other Pennsylvanians preceded him.

In 1883, for example, Thomas Struthers , a lawyer and land developer, constructed a multipurpose building in Warren, Penn., that contained a theater and storefronts. Those spaces were to support a public library that was also in the building. The business plan didn’t work, however, and users had to purchase “tickets” to borrow books.

Given such situations, Carnegie’s philanthropy was especially impactful because it shifted some financial responsibility to local governments.

While some of the lavish libraries Carnegie first erected in the Pittsburgh area came with endowments – the Homestead library is one that still exists – he later developed a formula to ensure that other communities would not rely on his continuous generosity. As a condition of most of his grants, Carnegie insisted that municipalities provide land plus annual operating funds equivalent to at least 10% of the buildings’ costs. This effectively committed municipalities to finance libraries with public dollars.

In Pennsylvania, rural residents received a library boost with the passage of Act 329 in 1931. The legislation offered partial matching funds to counties that provided library services.

Notably, the law excluded the state’s two largest counties – Philadelphia and Allegheny.

The federal Library Services Act of 1956-1962, a forerunner of the current Grants to States program, further aided libraries in communities with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants. The funds supported book purchases and projects such as bookmobile services.

Until the 1960s, though, there were no parallel funding streams for larger communities. This may have compounded other inequities.

Pennsylvania libraries did not practice de jure racial discrimination as Southern libraries did . Nor did they deliberately exclude senior citizens or people with disabilities. But how they allocated resources, designed spaces, developed collections, recruited staff and engaged local residents through specialized programming favored some constituents over others.

Just a few weeks ago I uncovered a November 1969 article in the Pennsylvania Library Association bulletin that was written by Augusta A. “Gussie” Clark , once a librarian and later a member of Philadelphia’s City Council. Clark wrote about how she believed white librarians in the City of Brotherly Love were failing Black children. She described the librarians’ lack of respect for Black communities, their “pained tolerance” of Black people in their midst, and an unwillingness to render extra help – all of which, she said, prevented Black children from feeling “at home” in public libraries.

Using libraries’ records, I have also found many requests from both individuals and advocacy groups asking for ramps, elevators and other alterations to century-old libraries, and for additional listening and viewing equipment. In at least one case, a complaint reached the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights; it was investigated and ultimately dismissed.

Libraries in urban areas of Pennsylvania began to receive state support after the passage of Act 188 of 1961, which created a state aid program for municipal as well as county libraries. It also provided additional funding to the Free Library of Philadelphia and Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, which became Statewide Library Resource Centers. As such, they received extra funding to provide services to other libraries and customers in the state.

On the national level, the Library Services and Construction Act , which replaced the Library Services Act in 1964, did not exclude urban and populous suburban areas as the Library Services Act had. In administering the new funds, the State Library of Pennsylvania approved many proposals that extended services to underserved residents, such as Montgomery County-Norristown Public Library’s outreach to public housing complexes and prisons , Altoona Area Public Library’s L.I.F.E. program for people with intellectual disabilities, and Cumberland County Library System’s STAR service for homebound senior citizens.

In the following decades, libraries continued to strive to become more accessible. In the 1990s the Library Services and Technology Act and state efforts such as Gov. Tom Ridge’s Link-to-Learn initiative addressed the digital divide between communities that had computers and internet connections and those that did not. It provided grants for libraries to acquire needed upgrades.

Thirty years later, there are still some places in Pennsylvania, especially in rural and mountainous areas, that don’t have broadband. However, that number shrinks each year thanks to federal and state efforts to build infrastructure in communities that corporate entities have neglected.

Some commentators argue that the internet, online databases and AI have replaced the need for public libraries and professional librarians. But a lot of information and recreational reading material is locked behind paywalls that Google and chatbots cannot circumvent.

Librarians today continue to play a crucial role in ensuring that resources remain available to the “largest number, at the least cost,” as American librarian Melvil Dewey articulated more than a century ago.

The Pennsylvania Library Association has found that for every $1 in tax investment, libraries return $5.50 in benefits . This is largely by acquiring materials at discounts and enabling library customers to share and reuse them.

Working in today’s libraries can require substantial courage, too, given current censorship trends in public libraries , including book bans . Requests to remove titles, or reshelve them in less-accessible areas, is nothing new. For example, I documented an example in Scranton in 1898 in which Catholic citizens urged the removal of Augusta Jane Evans-Wilson’s novel “Inez: A Tale of the Alamo,” due to its negative portrayal of a priest and inaccurate descriptions of Catholic sacraments. However, current activists’ tactics are becoming more broad-stroke, aggressive and even violent.

The American Library Association and EveryLibrary , a library advocacy group, have noted bills in various states that propose jailing library employees for the materials their institutions contain. There do not seem to be any bills presently of concern in Pennsylvania. But news reports about other book challenges and bans in Pennsylvania, especially in school libraries , regularly show up in my inbox and social media feeds.

When you view the centuries-long history of American librarianship through a Pennsylvania lens, it’s more complex, nuanced and fascinating than many people realize. And while today’s libraries face various challenges, I believe they continue to contribute enormously to residents across the entire state.

Read more of our stories about Philadelphia and Pennsylvania , or sign up for our Philadelphia newsletter on Substack .

titleEn: ‘The Uprising’ shows how medieval people weren’t so obedient after all
titleZh: 【arts】‘The Uprising’ shows how medieval people weren’t so obedient after all
descriptionEn: The English Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 wasn’t an isolated outburst. Across medieval Europe, ordinary people challenged the authority of rulers who failed to live up to their end of the bargain.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
For decades, I’ve been showing my medieval history students the “ autonomous collective ” scene from the 1975 film “ Monty Python and the Holy Grail .”

The clip is funny because it features two medieval peasants haranguing King Arthur while using the lexicon of a modern political Marxist. When Arthur explains that he was their king because the Lady of the Lake gave him Excalibur, one of the peasants objects: “Supreme executive power derives from a mandate from the masses, not from some farcical aquatic ceremony!”

It also subverts the assumption that medieval people were politically passive, with resistance to abuses of authority largely absent before the Renaissance and the Protestant Reformation.

But far from being an age of unquestioning obedience, the Middle Ages – the period from roughly 500 to 1500 – witnessed a remarkable number of popular revolts and collective political action.

Even if they didn’t speak in the language of Karl Marx, ordinary people back then held strong views about the working of political authority . And when they believed authorities had violated their obligations or lost their legitimacy, they routinely challenged rulers, bishops, tax collectors and urban elites.

In the 11th and 12th centuries, northern French peasants famously resisted carrying out the work or paying the money that they owed to the lords who controlled the land they farmed.

But perhaps the most well-known insurrection is the English Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 , the subject of the new film “ The Uprising ,” starring Andrew Garfield.

After the first wave of the Black Death in 1348 created a massive labor shortage in Europe, workers were better positioned to negotiate for higher wages and better conditions. Serfs – peasants bound to the land and subject to a lord’s authority – increasingly pushed back against oppressive feudal obligations.

But kings and lords resisted change. In 1351, England’s King Edward III decreed the Statute of Laborers , which froze wages, derailing any aspiration for social mobility among the peasant class. Resentment continued to build with recurring episodes of the plague.

Then, in 1381, Edward’s grandson and successor – 12-year-old King Richard II – instituted a one-time tax of 12 pence to raise funds for England’s ongoing war with France. Because the tax was charged per person rather than according to wealth, it placed a particularly heavy burden on poorer families.

The people had had enough: Crowds attacked tax collectors and eventually organized into a larger movement, burning houses, castles and the records that documented their obligations to their lords. They killed government officials before marching to London to confront the king.

The king met the rebels and pledged to abolish the poll tax and serfdom, while lowering the rent of agricultural land.

He later recanted those promises: His forces hunted down the rebels, quashing the uprising.

Insurrections like the English Peasants’ Revolt erupted, in part, because in cities across Europe, regular people had cultivated a strong tradition of collective action. There was broad membership in guilds , which were voluntary associations of merchants and craftsmen. Then there were neighborhood religious confraternities , which were akin to today’s religious mutual-aid societies. Together, they gave ordinary townspeople networks through which they could organize around shared interests and grievances.

Over in France, the Hundred Years’ War caused a breakdown in authority. People were increasingly being asked to pay taxes they couldn’t afford. Unpaid troops routinely raided the countryside, and the French military suffered a number of significant military defeats.

In 1358, the Jacques – a derogatory name for members of the lower French peasantry – razed noble estates and killed members of the aristocracy. They also joined forces with the Parisian bourgeoisie and the city’s chief political leader, Étienne Marcel, to fight for a greater voice in French government.

The rage underpinning the violence of what became known as the Jacquerie emerged from the fact that the same aristocracy that demanded so much of them could not fulfill their basic part of the bargain: protect them.

A little over a decade later, violence erupted in Florence, Italy. The city-state was an industrial juggernaut ruled by guilds, but their representatives all belonged to the urban elite. The lower classes of the textile industry weren’t represented by guilds and were largely disenfranchised. So the Ciompi – low-level woolworkers – demanded a role in the guild system. Those demands fell on deaf ears.

In June 1378, the Ciompi revolted and attacked government offices. Thanks to their efforts, they won participation in the guild system for four years, up until the city’s old powerful merchant elite dissolved their lower guilds.

Nor was the other main source of authority, the church, immune to attack.

When power vacuums emerged after the death of an abbot, bishop or even the pope, regular people routinely ransacked their property, taking with them a substantial amount of the dead’s movables.

“From various reports we are aware of the perverse and wholly detestable practice of certain people, who at the death of the bishop break in like enemies and rob his house, like thieves make off with his belongings, set fire to the homes on his estate, and with fierce and savage barbarity cut down his grape vines and orchards.”

Early Christian elections were initially open to entire congregations. Though these elections often gave the lion’s share of voting power to the wealthy and well-connected, there was the general understanding that everyone would play a role: “ vox populi, vox Dei ,” or “the voice of the people is the voice of God.”

However, by the end of the 13th century, the papacy had successfully established its authority over both ordinary people and secular rulers. On religious matters, there would no longer be public input. Instead, beginning in 1274, a conclave of cardinals elected the pope. The pope, sometimes still under the influence of higher lords, then nominated abbots and bishops.

The voice of the people had largely vanished. Nevertheless, they made themselves heard.

An April 1314 papal election in Carpentras, a small city in southeastern France, turned so violent that it delayed the naming of a new pope for nearly two years.

Deadlocked over the candidates, the cardinals dragged out the election for so long that frustrated locals attacked the episcopal palace where the conclave was being held. Cardinals and their staff fled and delayed until August 1316, when, under the protection of the French king’s forces, they nominated Pope John XXII .

Over 60 years later, in March 1378, Pope Gregory XI died. Amid threats from a crowd demanding an Italian pope, the cardinals elected Urban VI , an Italian, the following month. But over the ensuing months, the cardinals soured on Urban and declared their election invalid on the grounds that they had acted under duress. They elected a rival pope, triggering the Great Western Schism , during which two competing papal courts existed from 1378 to 1417.

Violence could also erupt for seemingly minor affronts.

In October 1367, Pope Urban V was in Viterbo, Italy. The pope and his court were French. The Viterbese took offense when papal court officials washed a little dog in their fountain of Piano di Scarano, which served as a source of drinking water. A confrontation followed, which escalated into a two-day uprising . The fountain was destroyed, and the pope and his cardinals were forced to take refuge in the Rocca Albornoz, the papal fortress.

Ideologies have evolved and technologies have advanced, but the fundamental struggle over who wields power, how authority earns legitimacy, and how compliance is enforced remains strikingly familiar.

The levers that leaders pull – taxation, welfare, infrastructure projects, propaganda, law enforcement – are largely the same, too.

Yet medieval folks understood that authority was a two-way street. When those in power didn’t hold up their end of the bargain, they were quick to resist, demand accountability and challenge authority.

In this sparring over power and consent, we can see, as one of Monty Python’s peasants put it, “the violence inherent in the system.”

titleEn: ‘Fountain’ might make you laugh or scowl but asks important questions – a Philly art historian explains why Marcel Duchamp’s iconic 1917 sculpture still provokes
titleZh: 【arts】‘Fountain’ might make you laugh or scowl but asks important questions – a Philly art historian explains why Marcel Duchamp’s iconic 1917 sculpture still provokes
descriptionEn: A version of ‘Fountain’ is part of the Philadelphia Museum of Art’s permanent collection and will appear in the Duchamp retrospective, which opens Oct. 10, 2026.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
Marcel Duchamp’s “Fountain” is not for everyone – and it does not need to be.

But it does encapsulate a central concern in the philosophy of art: What makes something art, and who gets to decide?

Whatever our tastes, art can challenge accepted systems and make us reconsider what we think we know.

Duchamp’s friend and chess partner John Cage observed in 1988 , “I can’t understand why people are frightened of new ideas. I’m frightened of the old ones.” “Fountain” embodies this thinking.

A version of “Fountain” is part of the Philadelphia Museum of Art’s permanent collection and will appear in the museum’s upcoming Duchamp retrospective , which opens Oct. 10, 2026, and runs through Jan. 31, 2027. The exhibition will revisit Duchamp’s enduring questions about what art is and what it can be.

As an art historian and former Philadelphia Museum of Art staff lecturer, I have developed an intimate knowledge of Duchamp’s art through years of teaching his work. During and after my tenure at the museum, I presented 101 lectures and led 25 gallery-based programs. Some of these focused directly on Duchamp, while others explored broader questions about originality, authorship, intention, skill and value.

These questions are embedded in the remarkable story of “Fountain.”

The 1917 original “Fountain” survives only in photographs, but 14 authorized full-scale replicas followed. The Philadelphia Museum of Art owns the earliest, signed by Duchamp in 1950.

“Fountain” continued a press narrative about Duchamp’s work that had begun four years earlier when his 1912 painting “ Nude Descending a Staircase (No. 2) ” became a sensation at the 1913 Armory Show in New York City. Journalist Julian Street remarked that it resembled “ the explosion of a shingle factory .”

Former president Theodore Roosevelt declared that a Navajo rug in his bathroom was “ a far more satisfactory and decorative picture ” than the cubist artists on display at the armory.

By 1917, Duchamp knew that controversy could compel audiences to debate what qualified as art. With “Fountain” that debate became part of the artwork.

Its story began with the Society of Independent Artists exhibition in New York in April 1917. Duchamp had helped found the society and establish its democratic premise that every member could exhibit without a jury. He tested that principle by purchasing a porcelain urinal, turning it on its side, signing it “R. Mutt 1917” and submitting it under a pseudonym.

The organizers excluded it from the official display and placed it behind a partition outside the main exhibition area. Collector Walter Arensberg, Duchamp’s friend and fellow board member, defended it and reportedly intended to purchase it . Both men resigned in protest.

Alfred Stieglitz photographed “Fountain” at his 291 gallery positioned in front of Marsden Hartley’s 1913 painting “ The Warriors .” The painting depicts a German military parade, and the title of the painting suggests a battle between old and new ways of thinking. Stieglitz’s photograph appeared in the May 1917 issue of The Blind Man , a short-lived New York avant-garde art magazine, alongside an editorial that argued that Duchamp’s act of choosing an ordinary object created “a new thought for that object.”

Duchamp called such objects “readymades,” a term historians believe he first used in a letter to his sister Suzanne dated Jan. 15, 1916. His first so-called readymade was “Bicycle Wheel” (1913), which joined an inverted bicycle wheel to a wooden stool. The lost original survives through replicas, including an authorized version from 1964 that’s held at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

“Bicycle Wheel” proposed that art doesn’t have to be handmade. An object can become art because the artist selects it and invites us to think about it differently.

Duchamp studied at the Académie Julian in Paris and was fully capable of traditional drawing and painting. He arrived at the readymades not because he lacked technical ability, but because he prioritized art that engaged the mind over what he called “ retinal art ,” art that primarily pleased the eye.

Seeing “Fountain” in Philadelphia provides a key to two of the museum’s other great Duchamp works: “ The Bride Stripped Bare by Her Bachelors, Even (The Large Glass) ” and “ Étant donnés .” The eroticism that “Fountain” implied with its associations to bodily functions evolved into frustrated desire in “The Large Glass.” In “Étant donnés,” the eroticism becomes explicit and voyeuristic, as it asks viewers to peer through holes in a weathered door.

Duchamp’s nod to manufactured plumbing systems in “Fountain” also anticipates his exploration of mechanical themes. In “The Large Glass,” the nine bachelors form part of an elaborate mechanical apparatus . In “Étant donnés,” an electric motor inside a cookie tin rotates a perforated disc, creating the illusion of a moving waterfall.

All three works shift art away from a self-contained image and toward an encounter involving object, idea, context, chance and viewer. “Fountain” transforms plumbing through the artist’s selection. “The Large Glass” incorporates chance through cracks created when it was shattered accidentally in transit – damage Duchamp repaired and embraced. “Étant donnés” incorporates found materials, including an old wooden door Duchamp obtained in Cadaqués, the Catalonian village where he and his wife, Alexina “Teeny” Duchamp, spent their summers.

Together, the works demonstrate that art can be a question to contemplate, a system to decipher, or an experience our actions complete. Seen together in Philadelphia, they reveal how consistently Duchamp made the viewer central to artistic meaning.

Despite its philosophical seriousness, “Fountain” is deliberately absurd and comical. It is appropriate to laugh. I’ve seen viewers even get angry and irritated. Its irreverent humor, provocation and rejection of artistic convention place it within Dada, a movement that began at Zurich’s Cabaret Voltaire in 1916 as an absurdist protest against the nationalism and supposedly rational values that had led to World War I. Dada became an international movement active in Berlin, Paris and New York, and it transformed modern art.

The legacy of the readymades, especially “Fountain,” is difficult to overstate. They paved the way for Louise Nevelson, who transformed discarded pieces of wood into monumental assemblages , and Andy Warhol, who elevated Campbell’s soup cans into icons of American culture. Maurizio Cattelan addressed Fountain directly in 2016 with “ America ,” a fully functioning toilet cast in 18-karat gold.

Nearly a century later, Cattelan echoed Duchamp’s questions about where artistic value resides: Is it in the object, its material, its price, its context, the artist’s idea or the institution declaring it art?

This leads to the great paradox of Duchamp’s legacy. Art conceived to challenge permanence, originality and inherent value has itself become permanent, invaluable and iconic.

Read more of our stories about Philadelphia and Pennsylvania , or sign up for our Philadelphia newsletter on Substack .

titleEn: The Women’s Professional Baseball League is betting that women’s baseball has a future in the US
titleZh: 【arts】The Women’s Professional Baseball League is betting that women’s baseball has a future in the US
descriptionEn: What will it take for the league to survive, expand and carve out its own identity in an increasingly saturated pro sports landscape?
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
Over 70 years after the dissolution of the All-American Professional Girls’ Baseball League – and nearly 30 years since the end of the short-lived Ladies League Baseball – female baseball players have been competing in a professional league of their own.

The Women’s Professional Baseball League began its inaugural season on Aug. 1, 2026, in front of a sellout crowd at Robin Roberts Stadium in Springfield, Illinois. Since then, the league’s four teams have battled one another across 30 games, producing highlight reel moments like Kelsie Whitmore’s three-homer game and Andréanne Leblanc’s walk-off grand slam .

The San Francisco Firebells finished the regular season atop the standings . The playoffs, beginning on Sept. 9, will determine the league champion.

The WPBL is appearing at a time when women’s sports in the U.S. are thriving.

Established leagues such as the WNBA and National Women’s Soccer League are seeing more investment, higher team valuations, lucrative media deals and growing fanbases. Women’s sports revenue is projected to reach roughly US$3 billion in 2026 – an increase of 340% in just four years.

The WPBL certainly hopes to capitalize on this moment. But the league is also doing something culturally significant: providing a pathway for the thousands of girls and women who choose to play baseball, not softball .

In the U.S., women have been playing baseball since at least the 1860s. But stubborn stereotypes continue to cast baseball as a sport for men and softball as the acceptable equivalent for women. Following legal challenges, Little League Baseball officially allowed girls to play in 1974. However, that same year, Little League Softball was founded, which steered girls away from baseball and reinforced the gendered split of the two sports.

Since then, there have been limited opportunities and resources available to girls and women in the U.S. who want to play baseball. Those who play Little League Baseball almost always switch to softball by high school. At the collegiate level, there are a handful of women’s baseball club teams , but it is not an NCAA-sanctioned sport.

Female ballplayers in other countries also face some of these issues. But I’ve researched and written about how developmental pipelines for women’s baseball players in Japan, Canada and Australia are far more established than they are in the U.S.

So it’s no surprise that nearly half of the 65 players in the Women’s Professional Baseball League hail from other countries, including 11 from Canada, eight from Japan, five from Mexico and four from Australia.

Japan’s Ayami Sato , picked second in the draft, is widely considered the best women’s baseball pitcher in the world. Thaima Maximiliana , from Curacao, was a first-round draft pick for Los Angeles, and South Korea’s Hyeonah Kim signed with Boston as the fourth overall pick.

That said, many of the American ballplayers had already made a name for themselves prior to joining the WBPL.

Kelsie Whitmore , who plays for the Savannah Bananas , a traveling team known for its entertaining style of play, was the league’s first overall pick. The Bananas play Banana Ball , a fast-paced variation of baseball with unconventional rules that puts spectacle and fan engagement at the heart of the game. Other women in Banana Ball to sign with the WPBL include Denae Benites , Val Perez , Ashton Lansdell and Mo’ne Davis , who became the first girl to pitch a shutout at the Little League World Series in 2014. Davis actually scored the WPBL’s first run .

The league also features women who play for the USA Baseball women’s national team , which recently qualified for next year’s Women’s Baseball World Cup.

Each WPBL team has a salary cap of US$95,000, so players will earn roughly $6,333 for the short, eight-week season. The league is covering housing costs and living expenses for the players, and they also receive a share of the league’s sponsorship revenue, in addition to any personal endorsement deals they might secure.

Even though the teams hail from other cities, all of the games for the inaugural season have taken place in Springfield, Illinois.

The location is symbolic: Springfield is where the first ticketed baseball game between two women’s teams, the Blondes and the Brunettes , took place in 1875.

In similar spirit, the team names commemorate trailblazing women. The New York Heights are named after civil rights leader Dorothy Height . The Boston Hunters pay tribute to Harriot K. Hunt , an influential medical doctor and women’s rights activist. The San Francisco Firebells honor Lillie Hitchcock Coit , a philanthropist and patron of the city’s volunteer firefighters whose nickname was “Firebelle Lil.” And the Los Angeles Queens are named after Lizzie Murphy, known as the “ Queen of Baseball .” Murphy was the first woman to play against Major League Baseball players when she faced Boston Red Sox players in an exhibition game at Fenway Park in 1922.

Meanwhile, the official league mascot is one of the most unique in professional sports: a dancing, cartwheeling version of Maybelle Blair , the 99-year-old former All-American Professional Girls’ Baseball League player.

ESPN Select has been broadcasting the entire season for the U.S. market, with select games also being shown on the Scripps Sports Network. Fans outside of the U.S. must tune in via YouTube.

Even though the regular season only included 30 games, there was plenty of drama on and off the field.

The manager of the Boston Hunters, former MLB All-Star closer Keith Foulke , was fired just three games into the season. Three weeks later, the league faced scrutiny after a board member filed a civil complaint alleging misuse of funds and conflicts of interest in the board’s makeup and hiring practices.

Yet play continued and proved exciting. San Francisco claimed the league’s first walk-off win in a game that featured two grand slams. New York’s Jaida Lee emerged as a top pitcher and led the league in strikeouts and strikeout rate. Whitmore and Benites finished the season leading the league with 11 home runs apiece .

Despite the success of its inaugural season, the WPBL is ultimately a startup that faces the challenges of any new league: It needs to grow its fan base, boost its media coverage, provide quality broadcasting and remain financially solvent.

So what will it take for the WPBL to survive, expand and carve out its own identity in an increasingly saturated pro sports landscape?

It’s worth looking to other emerging sports and leagues. Flag football is growing thanks to its inclusion as an Olympic sport and promotional and financial support from the NFL. Both Women’s Elite Rugby and the Women’s Lacrosse League hope to leverage increased interest and investment to succeed. And the Athletes United Softball League is utilizing its innovative rules to engage fans.

Questions linger about the future of the WPBL. But the league certainly has one thing in its favor: the rich history of women playing baseball, both in the U.S. and around the world.

titleEn: You can’t shield kids from scary news – here’s what ‘Sesame Street’ and other children’s shows did after 9/11
titleZh: 【arts】You can’t shield kids from scary news – here’s what ‘Sesame Street’ and other children’s shows did after 9/11
descriptionEn: Programs took different approaches to helping young viewers grapple with the horrors of the 9/11 terrorist attacks – lessons that still apply in today’s media environment.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
On back-to-school night in 2005, I eagerly entered my youngest child’s first grade classroom. The walls were festooned with brightly colored responses to the prompt: “Draw something you remember.”

I scanned for my son’s picture and was shocked when I encountered his drawing: an airplane flying into New York’s World Trade Center.

“I saw the picture you drew up on the bulletin board,” I said to him later that night. “Do you really remember seeing planes flying into the twin towers?”

He looked me in the eyes and replied, “No, Mommy. But I do remember you crying.”

My son was not quite 2 years old on on Sept. 11, 2001. As a mother, I despaired to learn that my own reaction to that day’s tragedies had stuck with him so viscerally. As a professor and researcher of children’s media , I shouldn’t have been surprised.

My son’s memory was likely influenced not just by my emotional reaction but by the media around him that his parents and siblings consumed in the weeks and years after the attacks – a mix of TV news and content geared toward kids.

More than two decades later, children have many more ways and more platforms to encounter frightening images and stories, often without an adult nearby to help them make sense of what they see. But the ways children’s programming such as “ Sesame Street ” responded to 9/11 offer a useful lesson: Rather than trying to shield children completely from disturbing events, adults can help them process what they’ve seen in honest, reassuring and age-appropriate ways.

Psychologist Joanne Cantor was one of the first to study what scares children about news and how they respond to it.

She concluded that what frightens children varies by their developmental stage . Younger children tend to notice and respond to stories about natural disasters and tragedies about kids or animals. Older children are afraid of stories focusing on personal injury and physical destruction, kidnapping, disease and violence. Teens express fear of stories about random acts of violence, natural disasters and foreign conflicts.

Since Cantor first published her groundbreaking research in the 1980s, kids’ media environments have changed dramatically, with more channels, screens and platforms broadcasting images and videos of natural disasters, violence and tragedies from around the world.

One study found that young children’s exposure to news is often accidental but lasting, with many children recalling distressing images long after the fact. Another one found that violent news images take a cumulative toll on children’s mental and emotional health. And an international survey of over 4,000 children from 42 countries found that over half had been scared by stories about the COVID-19 pandemic.

More recently, the children’s media nonprofit Common Sense Media surveyed hundreds of children ranging in age from 8 to 18 and found that what kids are seeing and hearing in the news frequently makes them feel scared, sad, angry or depressed.

On and after 9/11, millions of children like my son either saw the images of terrorist attacks or were near adults who reacted to them.

According to “Sesame Street” producer Lewis Bernstein , when the 9/11 terrorist attacks happened, most of the episodes for the forthcoming season were already written. Yet writers and producers knew that children were not oblivious – that even the 2- to 4-year-olds comprising the core “Sesame Street” audience had some sense of what was going on.

In response, the show’s producers collaborated with experts to create additional episodes that would address children’s fears.

In 2002, Rosemarie Truglio, vice president of education and research for “Sesame Street,” explained how the show’s approach was to meet children where they were developmentally.

“Sesame Street” had already helped children process their fears through classic episodes such as “ Grover’s Fear of the Dark .” Researchers knew part of what scared children on 9/11 were the loud sirens and the fact that trusted figures such as firefighters and police officers were hurt.

So the episode they developed in response to 9/11 made no mention of the terrorist attacks and instead centered on a fire at Hooper’s Store . Elmo is frightened by the noise of the fire alarm and subsequent sirens. The protective gear that the firefighters are wearing also scares him.

Fortunately, a kind and kid-savvy firefighter named Bill speaks to Elmo about his fears and invites him to visit the firehouse. There, he dispels some of Elmo’s concerns and dispenses advice about what children can do if they are ever in a similar situation.

The PBS show “Arthur” took a similar approach : Its two-part episode “ April 9 ” centers on a fire at Arthur’s school. It makes no mention of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks but explores how Arthur, Sue Ellen, Binky and Buster each process the school fire differently.

“Zoom,” the popular PBS live-action variety show, was geared toward older kids. Just 10 days after 9/11, they aired a special half-hour episode called “ America’s Kids Respond .” The seven cast members, all between the ages of 9 and 14, shared their thoughts, fears and feelings. Advisers knew their audience needed more than hearing other kids talk about their feelings. So they made sure the cast also discussed constructive things kids could do , such as helping with food donations or clothing drives for affected families.

A year later, “Zoom” followed up with another special, “ America’s Kids Remember ,” where cast members talked about how they had coped in the months after the attacks. They also read mail from viewers, including some letters written by kids who had been targeted by anti-Muslim slurs. The episode included a segment in which a cast member visited a girl in lower Manhattan whose school had been damaged. The girl explained how she was able to cope through her art and activism.

In 2001, most children under 8 were watching approximately 3.5 hours per day of television or videos on VHS .

Today, Common Sense Media reports that the amount of time kids spend watching television or videos is similar, but their total media exposure is far greater, thanks to mobile platforms and different types of media.

In a world where extreme weather events often lead local news, natural disasters routinely take place, and school shootings and acts of political violence have become all too common, parents might naturally try to shield children from these stories.

But young children pick up on the news and on cues from their parents, even when we don’t think they do.

There are many things parents and teachers can do to help mitigate children’s fears and anxieties from what they see on the news. Recognize some of the signs your child might be feeling anxious , such as sleep problems, avoidance of activities or doomscrolling. Experts suggest answering children’s questions honestly without necessarily relaying all of the gory details. It’s also OK to say, “I don’t know.”

Some of the lessons from how children’s TV dealt with 9/11 still apply.

Young children can also benefit from adults reassuring them that they are safe, by encouraging them to process a piece of news through play or art , and helping children by giving them language to express their questions and fears.

With older children and teenagers, experts suggest avoiding labels , such as blaming something on “the bad guys.” It’s important to give kids facts and context and provide them with resources to answer their questions. Older children can benefit from outlets to express their concerns and feel agency, whether through journaling or art, or the kind of volunteerism promoted on “Zoom.”

Finally, it’s important to acknowledge and explain our own emotions to our children, as I learned on that back-to-school night nearly two decades ago.

titleEn: How employers can make good decisions about remote work before the next crisis strikes
titleZh: 【business】How employers can make good decisions about remote work before the next crisis strikes
descriptionEn: Whether work gets done on-site, remotely or using a hybrid of the two can have a lot to do with an employer’s organizational culture.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
More than six years after the COVID-19 pandemic began, over 1 in 5 of the U.S. workers who can work remotely do so either full time or at least one day per week.

Even though a new normal has set in, no single approach has worked for all employees. And the debate over the benefits and drawbacks of remote work continues.

To see what factors affected the long-term shift to remote and hybrid work that kept going after the pandemic subsided, and to learn more about the pandemic’s effects on research firms more broadly, I teamed up with my Babson College colleagues , Gina O’Connor and Jonathan Sims .

We found that the process used to decide where employees should work matters just as much as the decision itself .

In early 2020, the research and development units of four global companies were conducting similar technical and scientific work. They all had access to the same communication technologies when COVID-19 upended everyone’s routine.

In keeping with social science research methods, we agreed to not name any of these companies. As we learned through a series of interviews with senior leaders, project team leaders and team members from 2021 to 2023, all four companies told most of their employees to work from home in March 2020.

What unfolded over the next three years in terms of how they arranged how and where employees would work as waves of COVID-19 came and went – remote, on-site or hybrid – differed in terms of the time it took them to arrive at stable work arrangements and the degree to which workers agreed with them.

Other research into how likely an employer is to allow remote and hybrid work arrangements after the pandemic has focused on executives’ traits, such as their age and personalities . But we’ve found that these choices regarding where employees work can have more to do with an employer’s organizational culture : the set of assumptions, beliefs and norms that shape how people who work together make decisions and interact with each other.

A Stanford University research team found in another study published in 2026 that the average percentage of paid full days worked from home shot from 7% shortly before the pandemic began to more than 60% soon after it started; the share of days spent working remotely then declined over the next two years to roughly 30%.

We noticed significant variations from this pattern among the four companies we studied.

For most scientists and technicians, fully remote work lasted between a few weeks and a few months. For the four companies we studied, it took 3-15 months to establish new stable work arrangements, sometimes with multiple workplace policy changes along the way.

Second, managers and employees understood, agreed with and accepted new work arrangements to very different degrees.

By early 2023, middle managers and workers at two of the four employers broadly accepted their companies’ work-from-home policies. At one of the other two, workers generally accepted it; at the other one, employees rejected the policies and were finding work-arounds to policies they disagreed with.

Because it develops slowly over years, organizational culture is hard to change. When a crisis strikes, that culture acts like a script that determines which decisions feel possible and which seem untenable.

We found that organizational culture determined how quickly an employer succeeded at establishing a new balance between remote, on-site and hybrid work after the earliest phase of the pandemic had passed.

Two of the employers established procedures and enforced clear lines of authority and rules regarding when employees could work from home. A research director at one of these highly hierarchical companies described the pandemic as “just another risk that needed to be managed” using existing protocols. These employers stabilized work arrangements quickly, and employees understood “the rules.”

The other two emphasized teamwork and participation, welcoming employee input in decisions. One of the two companies with collaborative cultures held workshops about the use of remote work, which included employees at every level – ensuring that all employees would understand what was being done and why.

Both kinds of cultures had strengths and weaknesses during and after the pandemic.

The hierarchical companies moved faster but struggled more with managerial issues over workplace policies when many of their employees felt their concerns were not heard. In contrast, the collaborative companies took longer to decide on their workplace policies but encountered less pushback from their employees.

Organizational culture can shape and limit an employer’s decisions during a crisis. Because developing a culture that is more flexible takes time, we believe employers should consider getting started on that process long before the next crisis hits and disrupts many work routines.

titleEn: The US sells more to Brazil than it buys – but Trump is slapping steep tariffs on its exports anyway
titleZh: 【business】The US sells more to Brazil than it buys – but Trump is slapping steep tariffs on its exports anyway
descriptionEn: Because Trump picked this fight due to his concerns about Brazilian politics, that country’s presidential elections might quell it soon.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
President Donald Trump has generally tried to justify his tariffs by asserting that they can help narrow the trade deficits the U.S. runs with most of the world . That argument is based on the fact that nearly all countries sell Americans more than they buy from the United States.

The U.S. announced a 25% tariff on Brazilian goods on July 15, 2026. A second measure, introduced eight days later, added another 12.5 percentage points on much of that trade. Both took effect on July 24, bringing the total to 37.5% where they overlap.

Here the imbalance goes the other way. U.S. exports to South America’s biggest economy have exceeded its imports for years. In 2025, American companies exported about US$54 billion in goods to Brazil , mainly refined fuel, aircraft parts, industrial machinery, fertilizer and electronics. They imported about $40 billion in Brazilian goods, mostly crude oil, semi-finished steel, coffee, orange juice, wood pulp, beef and passenger jets built by Embraer , the world’s third-largest aircraft maker.

In total, the U.S. ran a $14 billion trade surplus with Brazil.

Trump is discouraging Brazilian imports anyway. And this is his second attempt to do so. He announced a 50% tariff on Brazilian goods in July 2025, which the U.S. Supreme Court struck down in February 2026 , along with most of his other tariffs.

As scholars of international political economy who study U.S. trade policy and Brazil’s trade negotiations , we are researching why the U.S. imposed tariffs on Brazil despite Brazil’s trade deficit with the U.S., and how Brazil is responding.

In our view, this dispute was never really about trade. It began with Trump’s objections to a criminal case against former President Jair Bolsonaro – his political ally in Brazil. Today, with Brazil on the verge of a presidential election, standing up to Washington could prove a winning argument for the incumbent, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The administration spared 471 Brazilian products from the tariffs, among them coffee, wood and wood products, crude oil, natural gas, fertilizer, orange juice and pig iron. Most of the exempted goods are commodities and industrial inputs that American buyers would have trouble replacing quickly.

What stayed on the list is mostly manufactured: shoes, clothing, furniture, machinery and ethanol, the sugarcane-based motor fuel. Brazilian footwear and apparel, which compete on price in American stores, received no exemption at all.

While talks have deadlocked, in-person meetings are scheduled for Sept. 30 on the sidelines of a Group of 20 trade meeting in Wisconsin that will take place shortly before Brazilians go to the polls .

Goods worth a total of $94 billion moved between the two countries in 2025, far below the volume of U.S. trade with Canada, Mexico, China or the European Union. But Brazil ranks among the 17 biggest trading partners of the United States in terms of the flow of goods, ahead of Spain, Australia and Saudi Arabia.

The goods still facing tariffs are largely industrial inputs rather than shelf-ready products. So the cost of Trump’s tariffs is mainly landing on U.S. companies, which are the ones that pay when the goods arrive at the border.

Trump’s ability to use tariffs to push Brazil to change policies his administration objects to is limited because Washington’s trade-related leverage over Brazil has been shrinking for years. China surpassed the U.S. as Brazil’s largest trading partner in 2009 and has widened its lead since then. In 2025, China bought roughly 29% of Brazil’s exports and the United States only 11%.

The erosion of Brazil’s reliance on the U.S. market limits what Trump’s tariffs can accomplish. It helps explain why, when Washington slapped tariffs on imports from the whole world in 2025, Brazilian exporters could largely sell their wares elsewhere.

The pressure may be self-defeating. In August 2026, White House adviser Peter Navarro and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent published a report accusing about 40 economies, including Brazil, of helping China route goods around U.S. tariffs. Yet the more Washington restricts Brazilian access to the American market, the more attractive China becomes as a buyer of what Brazil’s selling.

Trump didn’t emphasize trade-related concerns when he announced the 50% tariff in July 2025. Instead, he criticized the criminal prosecution of former President Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally, which Trump has called a “witch hunt .” The U.S. government also accused Brazil’s Supreme Court of censoring American social media platforms within the South American country’s borders.

Bolsonaro, who once aligned Brasília with Washington, cannot run again because he is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup. But his son, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, is on the ballot.

Flávio Bolsonaro says he urged Trump not to impose tariffs. But his brother Eduardo, a Brazilian congressman, spent months in Washington lobbying the Trump administration to punish Brazilian officials over their father’s prosecution and welcomed the tariffs .

Even so, poll results point to a statistical dead heat between Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula. Another 13 minor candidates are also seeking the presidency.

After the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the Trump administration’s first round of tariffs, it tried using a different legal tool: Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. That law lets a president retaliate against foreign practices it deems unfair.

In the second trade investigation, the U.S. placed additional tariffs on Brazil and 59 other countries , which the Trump administration said had to do with the alleged use of forced labor in their supply chains.

Brazil initially lacked the means to respond to either round of U.S. tariffs.

But in 2025, Brazil’s Congress passed a new “ economic reciprocity ” law that borrows Section 301’s logic. It allows the executive branch to determine whether a measure taken by a foreign country harms Brazilian competitiveness. If it does, the government may impose tariffs as countermeasures or suspend intellectual property obligations.

Brazil opened its first case under that law on Aug. 13, 2026. It’s against the United States.

To be sure, launching a case does not guarantee that Brazil will retaliate. The procedure runs through seven administrative stages that together can take more than six months.

Brazil is also working on a slower, multilateral strategy. It has taken the dispute to the World Trade Organization , the Geneva-based body that writes and enforces global trade rules. The first stage of any WTO case is a round of formal talks called consultations, which the two governments are required to attempt before the dispute can go further.

Because the consultations with Washington ended in August without agreement, Brazil says it will request a formal WTO dispute panel , which would rule on whether the U.S. tariffs break the organization’s rules.

China has also joined that complaint, with India, Indonesia, South Africa, Colombia and Egypt signing on as interested parties.

We consider any official acts of retaliation against the U.S. by Brazil to be unlikely, due to the inherent power imbalance.

The U.S. consumer market is much larger than Brazil’s, and there are other asymmetries. The dollar-based financial system and Washington’s control over critical technologies give the United States ways to escalate trade battles that Brazil can’t counter. A trade fight could migrate to areas where Brazil has no way to respond in kind.

Canada’s situation shows what the alternative looks like. After its trade talks with Washington collapsed, Ottawa answered U.S. tariffs in August 2026 with tariffs of up to 50% on hundreds of U.S. goods , deepening a trade war between two countries that had been among the world’s closest trading partners. Canada sends roughly three-quarters of its exports to the United States , which gives its retaliation real bite – even if those tariffs may jeopardize its own economy. Brazil lacks that leverage.

Even if Brazil never retaliates, the steps it’s taking in that direction let the government show voters that it is doing something.

Lula’s approval ratings, which had been falling, recovered after he made national sovereignty the heart of his response to Washington. His officials say they don’t expect a deal with Washington to lift the tariffs before the Oct. 4 elections .

And whether Brazil ever activates its version of Section 301 to address what it sees as unfair trade practices may depend on who wins Brazil’s presidential election.

titleEn: US consumers and businesses are now facing a future of more expensive borrowing
titleZh: 【business】US consumers and businesses are now facing a future of more expensive borrowing
descriptionEn: The Federal Reserve’s rate hike comes as the US economy is increasingly moving at two very different speeds.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
From mortgages to auto loans to credit cards, borrowing is set to get even pricier.

But the Federal Reserve’s decision on Sept. 16, 2026, to hike its baseline interest rate also highlighted an increasingly confounding dilemma: It can raise the price of money across the economy, but it can’t determine which sectors are most affected.

That means the rate increase may further slow the weaker parts of the economy, such as housing , while barely affecting the strongest, namely the relentless investment in artificial intelligence.

In its statement summarizing its unanimous vote , the Fed’s policymaking committee said it was raising its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point so that it now stands at a new target range of 3.75% to 4%. It described inflation as still “elevated” and noted that other economic indicators remain strong, from productivity to investment, to domestic spending.

As a scholar of public finance , I believe the Fed probably had little choice but to raise rates given its commitment to maintain inflation-fighting credibility.
