Markets had already expected the hike, and if the Fed had failed to deliver, it might have pushed longer-term interest rates even higher amid concerns it was becoming less wedded to that target.

But the Fed’s action also underscores that the U.S. increasingly looks like an economy moving at two very different speeds. Investment in AI – whether through data centers, computing capacity or related infrastructure – has been booming, while it’s crowding out other kinds of investment.

Meanwhile, the housing market is getting crushed by high mortgage rates and diminishing affordability, while consumers are carrying ever more expensive credit card and auto debt .

Many small and traditional businesses are also in a bind as they face substantially higher financing costs than they did several years ago. Those costs reflect the rising yields on longer-term U.S. government debt, which have been going up for months on a mix of factors : Longer-term inflation concerns due to soaring U.S. government debt, geopolitical risks driving up energy costs, and ongoing financing demand for AI.

On Sept. 14, the yield on the 10-year Treasury crossed 5% for the first time since 2023.

When the Fed hikes short-term interest rates, it slows down economic activity by making borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive.

That mechanism works particularly well when consumers are deciding whether to finance a house, purchase a car or take on additional debt. It also discourages businesses from making investments when the expected return is only modestly above their financing costs. As demand slows, businesses have less room to raise prices, easing inflationary pressures.

In this case, the Fed justified its move by citing “elevated” inflation and noting that it “will support a timelier return” to its goal of an annual inflation target of 2%. It also suggested the economy would be able to absorb the tightening and described economic activity as “expanding at a solid pace.”

The decision aligns with Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh’s recent comments that restoring price stability is central to the Fed’s credibility. In a key speech in August, he underscored his commitment to bringing annualized inflation back down to 2%, an objective he called a “firm, fixed target” – a turnaround from his more ambiguous comments in July.

But in recent months, the economic data has shown that the 2% annual target remains elusive. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in August and 3.4% over the past year. Meanwhile, the war with Iran has pushed oil prices back above US$100 a barrel , adding a new source of inflation pressure through gasoline, diesel, transportation and production costs.

At the same time, the labor market isn’t faltering. The economy added 162,000 jobs in August , while the unemployment rate remained at 4.1%. The one notable concern is the persistence of long-term joblessness despite the strong headline numbers. More than one-quarter of unemployed Americans have now been out of work for at least six months.

Taken together, those numbers suggested there was room for the Fed to hike rates, given that the economy isn’t sliding into recession. So investors overwhelmingly expected the Fed’s rate increase.

However, tighter monetary policy carries a risk: It falls disproportionately on sectors that are already struggling and highly sensitive to interest rates, while having less effect on one of the economy’s strongest sources of demand – the booming AI investment cycle.

Housing provides the clearest example. Persistently high mortgage rates are reinforcing the “ lock-in ” effect for current homeowners. Millions of homeowners financed their houses when mortgage rates were 3% or 4%, so they’re staying put, with little incentive to sell their home and purchase another at much higher rates.

Mortgage rates are mostly influenced by longer-term factors , including Treasury yields, inflation expectations and market expectations about the future path of interest rates. But the Fed’s decision still matters. Markets increasingly expect today’s hike to be followed by additional increases, signaling that it views inflation as a more persistent risk and putting upward pressure on longer-term interest rates.

That expectation will keep mortgage rates high – probably resulting in fewer home sales, less mobility and continued headwinds for prospective buyers. It’s also likely to make renting relatively more attractive for potential homebuyers who are priced out of buying.

Higher-for-longer rates also change how consumers save.

When interest rates were near zero, they earned almost nothing on safe assets. Today, Treasury securities, money market funds and other relatively safe assets offer meaningful returns . Higher rates therefore tend to shift incentives throughout the economy away from borrowing and spending and toward saving.

With consumers stretched by inflation and increasingly dipping into their savings, however, this effect may be less pronounced .

When it comes to the AI investment boom, it’s a different picture. Warsh noted in August that more than half of recent capital-spending growth could be attributed to the AI buildout.

The companies that are spending billions of dollars on computing infrastructure are doing so because they expect potentially enormous returns from AI. If those expected returns on investment are exceptionally high, a modest increase in borrowing costs may do little to alter their investment decisions. That stands in sharp contrast to a prospective homebuyer getting sticker shock from mortgage rates nearing 7% .

The federal government, for its part, faces a slower adjustment. A Fed rate hike doesn’t immediately increase the interest rate on all outstanding federal debt. Most Treasury notes and bonds carry fixed rates until they mature. But as the Treasury issues new debt and refinances maturing securities, today’s higher rates gradually become tomorrow’s higher federal interest expense . That rise in interest costs is a main reason some economists are sounding alarms about the national debt, which recently topped $40 trillion.

In effect, the U.S. economy is facing a reality in which both short- and long-term rates stay higher for longer. The federal government, households and businesses are all adjusting to a borrowing environment that looks substantially different from the one that prevailed for much of the previous decade.

titleEn: To crack the job market, internships can be just as key for young people as the degree
titleZh: 【business】To crack the job market, internships can be just as key for young people as the degree
descriptionEn: Job preparation through internships matters more than ever for young people amid a precarious and fast-changing job market.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
College students are facing one of the most precarious labor markets in years. A recent New York Federal Reserve study pointed to a sharp increase in the post-college unemployed compared with other workers, with explanations ranging from artificial intelligence job displacement to a broader slowdown in hiring.

One response has been a boom in trade-school and apprenticeship programs that launch young people into “AI-proof” careers. But students at community and four-year colleges can also beat these headwinds and launch a career through on-the-job internships.

We’re a group of multidisciplinary scholars at The Ohio State University who study two paid internship programs in science, technology, engineering and math, or STEM, with a proven record of landing jobs for students. Although the two initiatives use different models, they both illustrate four lessons that colleges and employers can use to turn internships into genuine career pathways.

Just as notable is that a large share of these students come from diverse and underrepresented backgrounds, with many being the first in their families to go to college. These programs can serve as a powerful equalizer for young people who may not otherwise have such career opportunities.

Internships remain one of higher education’s most powerful tools for preparing students for work. Decades of research show that students who complete high-quality internships are more likely to secure job interviews and high-earning positions post-graduation.

At the same time, the number of internship opportunities is diminishing, even though that preparation matters more than ever. Artificial intelligence is transforming entry-level work , leading employers to increasingly value the human skills that machines cannot easily replicate: judgment, adaptability, collaboration and the ability to solve unfamiliar problems.

Academic leaders are recognizing these pressures. More than one-third of university presidents and two-thirds of community college presidents told an Inside Higher Ed survey that they plan to add or expand apprenticeship pathways over the next three years.

But it’s not just the number of internships that matters – internship quality counts just as much.

Our research at the College Impact Laboratory examined learning through experience with two multi-institutional studies. One is Bridging Academic Training Through Experiential Research and Innovation, or BATTERI , led by principal investigator Jay Sayre and project manager Joanna Gardner . The other is Drive to Thrive .

Across both initiatives, students benefited when their experiences combined substantive work with mentoring and professional development, rather than being treated as inexpensive labor. This distinction suggests that merely placing students in workplaces isn’t enough. The structure and quality of those experiences help determine whether internships lead to meaningful, high-earning careers.

Drive to Thrive deploys an approach called earn-as-you-learn. Through partnerships with Ford dealerships, students alternate between classroom instruction and paid workplace experience. They work alongside experienced technicians, diagnose and repair customers’ vehicles and receive regular coaching.

In this sense, it’s similar to the European model of traineeships for young people.

This initiative reached 635 students at 18 community colleges, including 345 first-generation students and 300 students of color. Through interviews and focus groups, a majority told us the internship helped them see themselves as true professionals. And several said the internship confirmed they had chosen the right career.

The numbers also backed up our approach. Students in the earn-as-you-learn program were almost 50% more likely to graduate compared with students in a matched comparison group.

Our other program brings together clean energy manufacturing students from three different types of institutions – a major research university, a historically Black university and a community college – for a 10-week internship. The program combines workplace learning with professional development workshops, peer networking, community engagement and projects with industry partners such as Honda, Stellantis and Schaeffler.

This initiative took a distinctive approach by assigning multiple mentors to each student. The idea is to help students develop relationships with faculty members, technical experts, employers and classmates. This network, in turn, strengthened students’ confidence, professional identity and sense of belonging while complementing the technical skills they develop.

To date, the formula has worked. More than half the participants in 2025 have already lined up either a new internship or job interviews. Industry partners also plan to rehire several members of the 2026 cohort as interns, extending their training beyond our program and opening pathways into clean-tech careers.

Based on this record, we believe that colleges should build broader support networks around internships rather than expect a single supervisor to shoulder the entire responsibility for a student’s professional development.

In both programs, four valuable principles emerged.

First is the importance of meaningful work. We believe interns should tackle real organizational challenges with deliverables that matter beyond the classroom. For example, two interns spent the summer addressing a safety challenge for Honda – how to prevent battery cells from catching fire and cooling them down when they do.

After developing potential solutions, they presented their work to industry representatives. A senior engineer from the Honda Research Institute was so impressed that he contacted them about a post-internship opportunity.

That sense of consequence changed how the students approached the work. Rather than viewing it as an assignment to complete, they were making a contribution that others depended on.

Second is the constellation of support for students. The liaison between the institution and industry partners is essential, serving as the connective tissue that holds the internship together and ensuring that students don’t fall through the cracks.

But that liaison alone isn’t enough. Students also need access to faculty, industry supervisors, technical experts and peers, since each brings a different kind of guidance. One strength of the clean energy program, for example, is its inclusion of industry experts across institutions and organizations. Students benefit most when they can draw on multiple mentors and peer support to develop key collaborative skills.

Third, students should learn how to normalize struggle. Internships aren’t a test of whether students can already function as professionals. They’re environments for students to try, fail and retry. When educators emphasize struggle as part of the learning process, students are encouraged to avoid perfectionism and instead ask for help when difficulties arise.

For example, students submit weekly reports during the clean energy program that give them the chance to discuss challenges, troubleshoot problems together and recognize that uncertainty is part of becoming a professional.

Finally, it’s vital to make interns’ contributions visible. Presentations, project showcases and recognition from industry professionals reinforce that students’ work matters while strengthening their professional identities.

We believe universities and industries alike should heed these lessons, which extend well beyond clean energy manufacturing and automotive technology. Successful programs build ecosystems that often determine whether students simply complete an internship or launch a career.

As colleges respond to changing labor markets, they should resist measuring success just by how many internships they create. Instead, they should ask whether those opportunities help students become confident, capable professionals. Internship quantity opens the door to better outcomes after college. Internship quality changes lives.

titleEn: How ‘portfolio reasoning’ explains Trump’s constant reevaluation of America’s value
titleZh: 【business】How ‘portfolio reasoning’ explains Trump’s constant reevaluation of America’s value
descriptionEn: Trump has approached governing through the same framework as his former business portfolio, where he casts the US as a flagship holding whose value he was elected to increase.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
In January 2026, President Donald Trump told an audience of business and political leaders in Davos, Switzerland, that the United States needed the “ right, title and ownership ” to Greenland “because you need the ownership to defend it. You can’t defend it on a lease.”

A territory of roughly 57,000 people appears to the president as property to be acquired.

Trump’s various actions during his second term have prompted no shortage of explanations. The “ flooding the zone ” strategy treats his flurry of executive orders and legal battles as efforts to overwhelm the courts’ and news media’s ability to keep up. Psychological explanations of Trump’s behavior point to narcissism . Other political commentators interpret his actions through authoritarianism and demagoguery .

I believe these accounts overlook something simpler. Before entering politics, Trump spent five decades running a commercial real estate business . In my assessment, he still reasons the way his professional career taught him to.

I study how forms of reasoning shape political arguments , and in analyzing Trump’s rhetoric across his second term, I find a president who approaches governing through the same framework as his business career – a mode of thinking I call portfolio reasoning.

Portfolio reasoning is a financial way of thinking that treats what one has – from property and money to relationships and obligations – as a collection of holdings to be continually managed and reassessed to maximize its value.

The recurring questions are familiar: What do I have? What is performing well and what isn’t? What should I keep, acquire, renegotiate or get rid of? And how do I make sure I can walk away?

Modern portfolio theory originated with economist Harry Markowitz in the 1950s as a way to manage financial risk. As finance came to dominate the wider economy, these habits spread well beyond Wall Street .

Consider a college sophomore today who, between classes, checks which stocks to hold or sell on the financial services platform Robinhood , reshuffles a fantasy football roster based on changing player values, and adjusts bets on future cultural and political events on a prediction market . Across very different activities, the same habit is at work: managing a shifting set of positions as their value changes.

It’s not difficult to imagine Trump’s second term through this lens.

According to portfolio theory, the soaring stock market, foreign investment growth and more tariff revenue become proof of the United States’ rising value . Previous presidents were bad negotiators who left money on the table. Alliances, treaties and obligations become holdings whose worth depends on maximizing their returns through continuous renegotiation. And states that vote the wrong way become candidates for divestment .

But a resemblance is not evidence. The more important question is whether Trump’s own words show that he reasons about politics this way.

Trump’s rhetoric repeatedly casts the U.S. as the flagship holding whose value he was elected to increase. He opened his 2026 State of the Union address by announcing that the nation was “back, bigger, better, richer and stronger than ever before.” The evidence that followed read like an investment performance report: The stock market had set “53 all-time record highs,” and the typical 401(k) was “up by at least $30,000.”

At a Las Vegas rally in August , he put it in the language of capital flows: “Money is pouring” into the U.S.

In Davos in January, in the State of the Union in February and again in Las Vegas in August, Trump described the country he inherited as a “dead country” that is now “ the hottest country anywhere in the world .”

It’s the language of a distressed property turned around.

Existing holdings get reassessed by Trump, too, and those judged to be underperforming are repriced.

In his State of the Union , Trump reported that NATO members had “just agreed, at my very strong request, to pay 5% of GDP for military defense rather than the 2%.” He added that the U.S. had been “paying the freight of many of them” and that NATO now pays in full for weapons sent to Ukraine.

Canada has faced the same reassessment. When it sought coverage under the proposed Golden Dome missile defense system, Trump put a price on protection – some $71 billion. He then offered an alternative : “Why don’t you just join our country? Become the 51st state and you get it for free.”

In this case, long-standing terms are reopened because one side can afford to walk away and the other cannot.

A portfolio also grows by acquiring what it doesn’t yet own.

Greenland is the clearest geopolitical example – Trump wants ownership , not access.

Venezuela follows a similar logic. After American forces removed President Nicolás Maduro , Trump announced that Venezuela would transfer up to 50 million barrels of oil . He said U.S. companies would go in and “start making money,” and noted that the country had been “pumping almost nothing by comparison to what they could have been” – an underperforming asset with a plan to improve it.

Not every acquisition is territorial. Since 2025, the federal government has taken ownership positions in roughly 30 companies , including 9.9% of Intel.

It’s fair to ask whether this is simply a more explicit version of what presidents have always done: pursue growth, expand power, defend the country’s interests.

Trump officials have suggested as much. White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller has described a world “governed by strength,” “force” and “power” – what he called “the iron laws of the world that have existed since the beginning of time.”

The difference has to do with limits – what stays open to negotiation and what doesn’t. Democratic governments may renegotiate treaties and alliances, but they also make durable commitments that are not continually reassessed according to what produces the best return.

Portfolio reasoning favors keeping your options open as circumstances change. Commitments are therefore provisional: Keep a position if it yields a high return, renegotiate if it doesn’t, and exit if something better comes along.

Trump applies that logic to nearly everything, leaving few political commitments settled and helping to explain the turbulence of his second term.

A second limit concerns the public. Viewed through a portfolio framework, people appear less as parties whose claims must be answered than as positions to be valued – assets when they contribute, liabilities when they don’t. Portfolio reasoning can assess value and risk. It cannot, by itself, distinguish right from wrong.

Applied to a population, portfolio logic does not necessarily deny human rights, but it offers no reason of its own for putting them beyond the reach of calculation. A portfolio presidency is not anti-democratic so much as indifferent: Democratic commitments have no privileged place in its financial calculations.

titleEn: AI is supercharging money scams – here’s what you can do to protect yourself
titleZh: 【business】AI is supercharging money scams – here’s what you can do to protect yourself
descriptionEn: Good habits by consumers can stymie scams, but US regulations have fallen behind the technology.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
The phone rings, and it’s your grandson’s shaken voice. There’s been an accident, he says, and he needs money before anyone finds out. Except it isn’t him. It’s software that learned his voice from a clip posted online, run by a stranger working through a list of phone numbers.

For years, warnings about artificial intelligence and cybersecurity have focused on corporate networks and government systems. Those threats are real. But if you follow the money in the FBI’s fraud data, a different picture emerges: Staggering sums are flowing out of household accounts .

In its 2025 annual report , the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center began tracking complaints with an AI connection for the first time. Americans filed more than 22,000 such cases and reported roughly US$893 million in losses. Investment fraud accounted for $632 million of that, and people over 60 accounted for $352 million of the losses.

Those figures include only victims who reported to the FBI, and only cases where AI’s role could be identified. The consulting firm Deloitte projects that the actual hit from AI will be much bigger and help push U.S. fraud losses overall to $40 billion by 2027, up from $12.3 billion in 2023.

I’m a finance professor who studies household finance and how people use AI to make money decisions . And I believe the most consequential AI security story right now isn’t unfolding in server rooms, but at kitchen tables.

None of these scams are new. What AI changed is the cost and the quality of the cons.

Cloning a voice now takes a few seconds of audio and cheap consumer tools. In one study , listeners were able to identify an AI-generated voice only about 60% of the time. Video is heading the same way. In 2024, a finance employee at the architecture and design firm Arup was tricked into wiring about $25 million to fraudsters after they set up a video meeting “staffed” by deepfakes of the chief financial officer and several colleagues.

Phishing has improved, too. Clumsy wording and odd formatting used to give fraudulent emails away. Language models now write clean, fluent messages and can personalize them at scale using details scraped from social media. Deepfake videos of well-known business figures pitch bogus trading platforms.

The same pressure is visible in business losses. The cyber insurer Resilience reported that more than 85% of the losses in its claims portfolio in the first half of 2026 stemmed from attacks aimed at people rather than systems.

We’d like to believe that only careless people get taken. Research in behavioral finance says otherwise.

These scams are engineered around fear and urgency: a panicked grandchild, a boss demanding a same-day transfer, an investment window that closes tonight. Stress narrows attention and pushes people toward fast, intuitive judgments at the very moment they need slow, deliberate ones. Fraudsters also strike a pose of authority, whether a CFO’s face or a government agency’s letterhead, because most people defer to it.

Fluency matters as well. My own research examines how the smoothness of AI-generated communication leads people to trust it. A message with no typos, in a voice that sounds exactly right, sails past defenses that a clumsy fake would have tripped.

Nobody plans to make a major financial decision mid-panic. That’s exactly why scammers manufacture the panic.

AI-enabled theft doesn’t necessarily involve talking to the victim. Stolen personal data sells for a few dollars on dark web markets. Criminals then feed it to automated AI agents that probe bank and fintech systems around the clock, testing credentials and hunting for weak points at a speed no human crew could match. Last fall, the AI company Anthropic disrupted an espionage campaign in which an AI agent performed 80% to 90% of the intrusion work against roughly 30 targets, including financial institutions.

When an attacker gets into a customer account, the takeover can be over in minutes. Instant payment platforms like Zelle, built for speed and convenience , become the getaway car. The money typically moves within minutes, and getting it back is almost impossible.

Banks defend their own wire rooms with procedures, not vigilance. Households can borrow those procedures.

Check by calling back. When you get a suspicious call , hang up and dial a number you already know – like your bank’s fraud hotline – and never one the caller or message supplies. The point is to leave the channel the scammer controls. A cloned voice can’t answer your grandson’s real phone.

Trust and verify. You should agree on a robust family code word for emergencies and treat any request for money that lacks it as fake. Require two people in your household to sign off on any large transfer, so nobody moves serious money alone and under pressure. And build in a delay, such as a self-imposed 24-hour wait, before any big payment. Urgency is the scammer’s tool. Slowness is yours.

Add layers of protection. Protect the accounts themselves, too. Turn on two-factor login for financial accounts, and never share a verification code with someone who contacts you. That code is the second lock on your door, and the only reason a caller wants it is to get in.

You should also switch on your bank’s transaction alerts so a takeover announces itself in minutes, and consider a credit freeze , which is free and blocks thieves from opening new accounts with data bought on the dark web.

Protect older people. With $352 million of reported AI-related losses coming from Americans over 60, conversations with older family members are key. Walk through the callback rule and the code word, and ask their bank or brokerage about adding a trusted contact they can call. It costs nothing, and it gives the institution a way to raise an alarm before the money moves.

If money has already moved, you should call your bank immediately, ask it to attempt a recovery, then report the scam to the Federal Trade Commission .

Good habits raise the cost of every one of these scams, but they can’t do it all. This is where the U.S. regulations have fallen behind the technology.

Federal law is supposed to protect consumers from unauthorized electronic transfers, and regulators have said that a transfer set in motion by a fraudster counts as unauthorized even when the victim was tricked into handing over account credentials.

In practice, though, victims of instant-payment fraud often recover little . Banks frequently classify losses as “authorized” when a customer was deceived into approving the payment, and even obvious victims of such takeovers can face long fights over reimbursement.

For example, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Zelle’s operator and three of the country’s largest banks over their response to alleged fraud in late 2024, then dropped the case in March 2025. New York’s attorney general has since filed her own lawsuit, which a judge allowed to proceed in July . Zelle’s operator denies the allegations and says it will appeal.

The U.K. has taken a different path. Since late 2024, U.K. banks have been required to reimburse most scam victims up to £85,000, roughly $115,000, with the cost split between the sending and receiving institutions. The logic is that banks are best equipped to fight fraud, since they run security teams and networkwide analytics that can spot suspicious patterns across millions of transactions. What they had lacked was a strong financial reason to deploy them fully, and the reimbursement rule supplied it.

The regulator’s own dashboard shows that 88% of the money lost to eligible scams has been returned to victims since the rules took effect. More telling: An independent evaluation found that scam losses fell by roughly a fifth in the rule’s first year. That shows that when banks bear the losses, they find ways to prevent them.

I believe American regulators and Congress should study that model closely. When payments are instant and irreversible, the risk cannot rest almost entirely on the customer, who is the least-equipped party in the chain.

titleEn: Why the Trump administration’s bid to end diversity efforts at nonprofit schools is likely to get tied up in court
titleZh: 【business】Why the Trump administration’s bid to end diversity efforts at nonprofit schools is likely to get tied up in court
descriptionEn: A proposed Trump administration rule aimed at quashing diversity efforts could jeopardize the nonprofit status of private schools. It could take effect in mid-2027.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
The Trump administration wants to strip all nonprofit colleges, universities and private K-12 schools of their tax-exempt status if any of their programs designed to help students uses race as a criterion for eligibility.

This change is included in a rule the Treasury Department and Internal Revenue Service proposed on Sept. 3, 2026 . The rule could take effect after May 31, 2027, following a two-month-long comment period – as long as it’s not blocked or delayed by the legal challenges likely to arise.

As a nonprofit law scholar who helps nonprofit leaders understand the legal issues they face , I believe this latest salvo in the Trump administration’s attempt to end racial preferences stretches U.S. law so far that it will likely be tied up in court for years.

The proposed rule states that private schools aren’t eligible for tax-exempt status if they have any school-administered or -supported program that “discriminates on the basis of race, color, or national or ethnic origin … for any purpose.”

The regulations do not define the word “discriminate” in this context, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has made clear that the Trump administration considers programs that have diversity goals to be a form of discrimination.

Private K-12 schools, colleges, universities and professional and trade schools would be subject to this rule, including all academic and athletic programs as well as all scholarships and admissions policies having anything to do with efforts to increase diversity.

The proposed rule would not apply to religious schools that make admitting people who adhere to the school’s religion a priority. Nor would it apply to public universities, but I believe the language is broad enough to apply to the foundations that provide scholarships to students at public universities.

At this point, many key details about the rule remain unclear.

The IRS estimates that this rule would affect 18,000 private schools attended by 750,000 students at all levels of instruction.

All private schools that are nonprofits depend on this tax exemption, both to save money on income and property tax bills and to attract donations . Without these benefits in place, tuition bills at nonprofit schools could skyrocket and the financial pressures many colleges and universities already face would increase.

Americans gave about US$92 billion in charitable donations to private schools in 2025, which mostly supported higher education. That funding covers an average of about 10% of college and university budgets .

A change in the rules could also complicate schools’ relationships with their donors, alter the distribution of scholarships and lead to significant legal bills, as the government itself has acknowledged .

The proposed rule hinges on the Trump administration’s definition of racial discrimination: that any kind of racial preference is wrong and grounds for terminating government support – even when it’s meant to address past injustices, like the decades of systemic discrimination that followed the end of slavery in the United States.

The IRS’ explanation of this rule alludes to many legal precedents, including two significant U.S. Supreme Court decisions.

With its Bob Jones University v. United States ruling, the court found in 1983 that a university banning interracial dating and marriage provided the IRS with the legal grounds to revoke its tax-exempt status .

And the court found in 2023, in its Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard ruling, that colleges and universities that accept government funding cannot consider race in their admissions policies without violating the equal protection clause of the Constitution.

There is evidence that the government lacks the authority to implement this proposed rule.

Educational groups, such as EdTrust and the American Association of University Professors , have expressed their opposition to the proposed changes. Legal scholars, such as Philip Hackney, Ellen Aprill, Daryll Jones and Brian Galle , have explained why the rule is likely illegal.

Two courts found on June 30, 2026, that the Department of Education did not have the authority to alter student loan forgiveness rules for the employees of nonprofits . I expect to see opponents of the proposed rule to use those cases to support this argument.

Even if the courts determine the IRS does have authority to issue this rule, they will have the final say as to whether the agency has interpreted congressional intent correctly.

Legal scholars are also saying that the Trump administration’s interpretation of prior Supreme Court cases regarding discrimination at schools with tax-exempt status is incorrect.

They point out that the Harvard admissions case was limited to colleges and universities that accepted public funding, and it provided some narrow exceptions. The proposed regulation would apply to all private schools, without exception, even if they don’t receive federal funding.

Further, the Bob Jones ruling stressed that a nonprofit’s tax-exempt status could only be revoked on “fundamental public policy” grounds when the activity in question so shocked the community conscience that it undermined any other benefit the institution conferred. It based its opinion on 30 years of evidence from all three branches of government to show that this kind of prejudice violated fundamental public policy.

The Trump administration may be unable to show that the public’s perspective regarding diversity, equity and inclusion has changed that much. It faces numerous lawsuits challenging its definition of racial discrimination, and the American public remains overwhelmingly in favor of diversity, equity and inclusion policies.

Law professor Roger Colinvaux has also pointed out that interpreting the term “discrimination” to mean that organizations can no longer remedy past discrimination runs counter to the legal definition of the term “charitable,” which means to help those in need. Treasury Department regulations define charitable activities as helping “the poor and disadvantaged” and eliminating “prejudice and discrimination.”

Finally, as Alexander Reid, a prominent attorney who specializes in tax exemptions, noted in a letter to the IRS , the proposed rule raises significant First Amendment issues of freedom of speech , religion, association and institutional autonomy. That’s because it would affect choices that all private schools make that are essential to their identities and expression of ideas.

Two years ago, the federal government supported a definition of racial discrimination that is vastly different from the definition the Trump administration now holds, and a new administration could come up with still another meaning. The lawsuits that will surely challenge this proposed rule will help to determine the legal meaning of racial discrimination – and Congress could weigh in as well.

In the meantime, many nonprofit schools may end their programs that are designed to address the results of past discrimination out of a fear of potentially losing their tax-exempt status.

I would not be surprised to see other kinds of nonprofits taking similar precautions as well, on the assumption that the Trump administration will apply this logic more broadly in the future.

The IRS will need to respond to the major themes addressed in the comments it receives by Nov. 3, 2026. It may change the rule before it issues a final version.

And even if the rule were to be finalized on schedule, I would expect extensive litigation could delay or prevent its implementation.

titleEn: How diaspora groups in the US are responding to disasters in Nepal, Colombia, Venezuela and other homelands
titleZh: 【business】How diaspora groups in the US are responding to disasters in Nepal, Colombia, Venezuela and other homelands
descriptionEn: While small in scale, these groups are well positioned to respond quickly to disaster relief efforts.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
A string of major disasters in 2026 have had devastating consequences. Earthquakes in Venezuela and Colombia and floods and mudslides in Nepal have killed tens of thousands of people and injured many more. Countless people remain missing and hundreds of thousands of homes are damaged, with some entire neighborhoods destroyed.

The responses have been global. For Nepal alone, the United Nations Global Emergency Fund has allocated US$2 million, while the U.S. has committed over $3 million and the European Union has sent just under $3 million. Big humanitarian organizations such as Direct Relief and Save the Children have started fundraising campaigns to support the response efforts in Nepal.

Among the first to respond have been support groups set up by people originally from countries hit by disaster but now living elsewhere.

While small in scale, these diaspora groups are well positioned to respond quickly to disaster relief efforts. They have developed partnerships with community groups on the ground in their home countries. They also have a strong pool of donors – among the diaspora and beyond – based in the U.S.

I study philanthropy and nonprofits and research diaspora-led nonprofits. These organizations play multiple roles. They support other people in their immigrant communities in the U.S. and engage in the preservation of their cultures while living far from their homelands. Increasingly, they also respond to urgent needs in their countries of origin.

The money people living abroad send to their relatives and friends back home is called remittances . Globally, more than $900 billion flows across borders annually this way.

Diaspora communities are also playing a growing role in development aid and giving in response to disasters in many countries. This is additional money beyond that $900 billion; no authoritative estimate is available.

The Nepalese diaspora groups that have responded are less visible. But nonprofits led by Nepalese people who live in the U.S., like the Nepali Association of Oregon , the Albany New York Nepalese Society and Nepalese Aid , are gathering donations to send back to their homeland.

Likewise, after the June 2026 Venezuela earthquakes, Venezuelans living abroad , including business owners , and organizations led by Venezuelan emigrants, such as Venezuelans and Immigrants Aid , have mobilized.

My research shows that diaspora-led nonprofits are able to quickly respond when disasters strike because of the partnerships they have already forged with community groups in their homelands.

For instance, I found that Colombian diaspora-led organizations have ongoing projects in areas that range from education to nutrition. They can ramp up to expand their philanthropy when a disaster occurs .

Give to Colombia , a nonprofit based in Miami-Dade County led by Colombians living there, has swiftly dispatched relief funds before. In November 2020, the Category 4 Hurricane Iota hit Colombia’s Providencia Island. The storm damaged 98% of the island’s infrastructure, and an estimated 40% of the 5,000-plus inhabitants were displaced to other parts of the country.

Organizing with its partners, including the Colombian-based nonprofit Presentes Corporation , Give To Colombia created Stand Up: Providencia Reborn . In 2020, the initiative raised $500,000 to build a community center and reconstruct local inns to help over 1,000 Colombians rebuild their tourism businesses.

Give To Colombia and Presentes Corporation have teamed up again in response to the 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck the Chocó region of Colombia on Aug. 10, 2026. Together they have launched Colombia Se Levanta , meaning “Colombia rises up,” to raise money to help pay for recovery and rebuilding efforts.

Most diaspora-led nonprofits have a committed base of volunteers and donors. In the case of the Albany, New York, Nepalese Society, there are more than 600 Nepalese whom the nonprofit is calling on to give in response to the mudslides.

When I studied Mexican hometown associations , I found that those groups typically had anywhere from 20 to 500 active members, with around 3,000 associations in the United States .

I’ve also found that diaspora leaders take pride in their philanthropy.

A Colombian immigrant who helped to create New England Association for Colombian Children in the Boston area told me, “I do not plan on returning to Colombia now, the U.S. is my home. But I get great fulfillment from giving back to the place where I was born.”

She encourages other Colombians living in the U.S. to learn about the organization and to give their time and money to causes in Colombia. As a result, the group has become a magnet for many Colombians who end up in the Boston area.

In addition, diaspora-led organizations deliberately involve young immigrants, whether they came as children to the U.S. or were born to immigrant parents.

This can help expand the donor base of these groups, even when there’s no disaster to respond to. The India Philanthropy Alliance’s annual Youth Essay Competition is a good example of this. It calls on middle and high school students, often Indian Americans, to write essays that identify social challenges facing India and propose solutions.

To be sure, the funds that these diaspora-led nonprofits raise can be modest in comparison to other efforts. Give to Colombia is close to reaching its target of $300,000 in response to Colombia’s 2026 earthquake. The New England Association for Colombian Children also has a campaign underway, Colombia, Estamos Contigo , meaning “We’re with you, Colombia.” It has already surpassed its target of raising $25,000.

Still, I believe these diaspora-led nonprofits have staying power, given the deep sense of connection that they have with their homelands. They will be ready to respond whenever new disasters occur.

titleEn: Learning another language may be one of the best ways to keep your brain healthy as you age
titleZh: 【education】Learning another language may be one of the best ways to keep your brain healthy as you age
descriptionEn: Learning another language is not a miracle cure for aging, and it cannot guarantee protection against Alzheimer’s disease. But it does have various other benefits.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
Learning another language is a highly complex mental activity . It requires people to remember words, distinguish unfamiliar sounds, recognize patterns, work out grammatical rules and retrieve the right expression at the right moment. All of this happens while listening, interpreting and preparing a response.

Could all this mental activity also help keep an aging brain healthier ? Research suggests it can .

Concerns about memory and dementia can send aging adults looking for ways to exercise their brain and maintain cognitive function, whether it is solving crossword puzzles or playing a musical instrument. Language learning might not seem like the same kind of brain exercise, but it is a complex activity that engages several mental processes at once.

I am a linguist who studies language acquisition, use and loss. My new book, “ Beyond Words: How We Learn, Use, and Lose Language ,” examines language and the mind across people’s lifespans.

Research increasingly suggests that language learning and bilingualism can offer cognitive benefits – including for older adults. Learning another language can also create opportunities for communication and social connection.

A person’s brain remains capable of change throughout their life. This ability to adapt in response to experience is known as neuroplasticity.

Learning unfamiliar sounds, vocabulary and grammatical patterns requires the brain to form and strengthen connections. Language learning engages several mental processes at once, requiring people to absorb and retrieve information , notice when something does not work out, and adjust . This sustained mental effort makes language learning a particularly rich form of cognitive exercise.

Research on bilingualism has found differences in both the brain’s gray matter, which contains neurons and their connections, and white matter, which consists largely of nerve fibers linking different parts of the brain.

Studies have shown greater gray matter density or stronger white matter integrity in bilingual people , compared with people who speak one language. These findings suggest that language experience can be reflected in the brain’s structure, as well as its activity.

But brain differences are only part of the picture.

One reason researchers are interested in language and aging is the idea of cognitive reserve . This term refers to the ability to maintain cognitive function despite age-related changes or damage to the brain.

Bilingualism has been proposed as one factor that can help the brain cope with the effects of aging, because managing two languages places ongoing demands on people’s attention and cognitive control – ultimately helping to strengthen cognitive reserve.

Some studies have found that bilingual people who develop dementia show symptoms at a later age than people who speak one language . This suggests that bilingualism may provide some protection against the effects of brain aging, although it does not necessarily prevent dementia or the brain changes associated with it.

The potential benefit may therefore be greater resilience in the face of those changes, rather than prevention of the underlying disease.

This raises another question: If lifelong bilingualism may help protect the brain as we age, can people gain similar benefits by learning a language later in life?

Age changes the way languages are learned, but adults remain capable of learning new languages throughout life. Adults and kids bring different strengths to the task. Children tend to have advantages with pronunciation and some aspects of grammar, while adults bring larger vocabularies and better-developed strategies for learning.

Research involving older adults suggests that learning a language can produce cognitive benefits, although the findings are mixed . The potential benefit may come less from achieving fluency than from the process of learning itself. Language learning is a sustained challenge that keeps people learning, practicing and adapting.

There are social benefits, too. Learning another language can deepen cultural understanding , improve interpersonal communication and encourage people to empathize with other people’s perspectives and experiences. It can also connect people with others from different linguistic and cultural backgrounds, creating opportunities for conversation and friendship.

There is no established formula for how much language learning is needed to provide these benefits. Studies have used everything from intensive classroom instruction to short daily sessions with language-learning apps, over periods ranging from weeks to months, to see whether language learning can improve cognitive function. Rather than a magic number of hours, what matters may be sustained engagement in a challenging activity like learning a new language.

Learning another language is not a miracle cure for aging, and it cannot guarantee protection against Alzheimer’s disease or other forms of dementia.

But it is an unusually rich form of mental activity .

Perhaps the most useful way to think about language learning is not as a way to keep the brain young, but as a way to support cognitive resilience – the ability to keep learning, adapting and functioning despite the changes that come with age.

Aging inevitably changes the brain, but people retain the capacity to learn throughout life. Keeping our brains engaged in demanding new activities may contribute to that resilience.

titleEn: Lockdown or active shooter drill? The distinction matters for children’s safety and well-being
titleZh: 【education】Lockdown or active shooter drill? The distinction matters for children’s safety and well-being
descriptionEn: Lockdown and active shooter simulations look and feel very different, though people often lump the two practices together.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
School shooting preparedness drills have been a routine though uncomfortable part of the back-to-school experience. Since the 1999 mass shooting at Columbine High School in Jefferson County, Colorado, various kinds of preparedness drills have been mandatory in most schools.

As schools schedule and conduct these preparedness exercises, parents are likely to hear grim terms like “ active shooter drill ” and “ lockdown drill .”

For most schools, these drills are not optional. As of 2025, 37 out of 50 states require schools to conduct active shooter or lockdown drills at least once per year. Some states, like New York , require schools to conduct lockdown drills at various points throughout the year. Texas, meanwhile, requires lockdowns and shelter-in-place drills, but it also permits active shooter threat exercises, including shooter simulations.

The nationwide controversy over school shooter preparedness drills tends to conflate hyperrealistic simulations – with fake blood and bullets – with lockdown procedures, which might involve turning off the lights and having children remain quiet.

While research is mixed on the effectiveness of both kinds of school shooter preparedness exercises, the two practices look and feel very different.

A lockdown drill typically involves three simple elements: locks, lights and moving out of sight.

Teachers and students learn to lock their classroom doors, shut off the lights and move to a safe area without sight lines until an all-clear notification from a school official or police.

Carrying out this routine can build familiarity and muscle memory that encourage a rapid and calm response in the event of an actual emergency.

Lockdowns may be initiated for any number of reasons, not necessarily related to an active shooter. A student once told me that the single lockdown she experienced in elementary school was in response to a squirrel that had invaded the building.

Other schools have been forced to implement lockdowns for graver threats: parent disputes that become physical , nearby police activity , wildlife , or, in the worst-case scenario, an armed assailant .

Active shooter simulation drills, meanwhile, are specific to armed assailants.

These drills may involve actors posing as shooters, as well as mock gunfire, fake blood, and even the use of nonlethal projectiles, such as BB guns or paintball guns.

Among surveyed K-12 teachers, 55% reported that the active shooter drills practiced in their schools did not include sensory elements such as fake blood. Yet around 6% of teachers had experienced drills with simulated gunfire, and 1% reported fake blood or explosions.

High-intensity simulations are restricted in some states, including New York and California.

Other states may explicitly differentiate between active shooter simulations and lockdown drills. Many states have no guidelines at all related to simulations in schools.

Still, research shows there are significant concerns about the psychological harm these simulations can have on students and teachers. Importantly, there are no existing studies that test whether they improve outcomes in real-world active shooter scenarios, because the baseline rate of these attacks is so low.

Yet these drills tend to generate the most media attention and public outcry .

Moreover, they are conflated with lockdown drills, leading to parents hearing about lockdown practices and drawing parallels to terrifying simulations with pretend shooters and gunfire.

When federal sources report that 95% of U.S. schools implement lockdown drills, this mostly refers to locks, lights and out-of-sight practice – not simulations and armed assailant drills.

The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine cited this 2023 statistic in an influential report on the mental and emotional risks of active shooter drills , but ambiguously presented that “95%” as reflecting “active shooter drills,” not lockdowns.

Unsurprisingly, this report found mixed results on the impact of active shooter drills. The report also revealed a lack of standardization across schools for drills and preparedness in general.

This has made it nearly impossible to understand what is harmful, what is helpful, and what should be common practice.

Professional organizations warn that high-intensity active shooter simulation drills may cause trauma for students , without making them more prepared for such a terrifying, real-life situation.

But academic studies have found some support for lockdowns .

For example, middle and high school-aged students in a large, urban central New York school district reported lower fear and better preparedness after participating in lockdown drills with the locks, lights, out-of-sight approach.

Other studies assessing various exercises , ranging from lockdowns to active shooter simulations, report mixed and negative impacts on fear and anxiety.

This indicates a fundamental problem with how we study preparedness drills: The research itself lacks the nuance required to establish clear harm or benefit to practicing for an active shooter situation.

Observational studies suggest that lockdowns can impede shooters’ movement through space, potentially mitigating harm. Research from Texas State University has found that unsecured doors were associated with more victims during active shooter incidents at schools.

A separate study suggested that lockdowns are associated with fewer casualties during mass school shootings.

At the start of the 2026-27 school year, a parent posting on the subreddit “Daddit” shared a story about his preschool-aged child practicing staying quiet so “the bad guy” would not hear her.

This kind of scenario is simply not needed, research shows. As children age into middle and high school, lockdown practice is paired with the rationale for the drill, incorporating more sophisticated discussions about school safety, violence prevention and response, and emergency preparedness.

In early childhood and beginning elementary school, the routine can be learned without the rationale or explanation.

The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that adults running these drills use neutral phrases like “lockdown” or “safety drill,” instead of a more frightening term like “active shooter drill.”

Some schools follow this guidance, but others may not.

My preschooler has informed me of “quiet times” when he and his classmates sit in a corner and learn to stay quiet. When gently prodded for more explanation, he has no other reasoning for the behavior except that it is a time to be still and quiet.

There is cautious consensus among experts that some kind of intruder preparedness is necessary.

When conducted with the procedural simplicity of fire drills, lockdowns may be the least traumatic and most effective drills. Just as fire drills rarely simulate actual fires, lockdown drills need not introduce harmful or deceptive scenarios that explicitly recreate an emergency.

But with a lack of standardized practice, guidelines and terminology, disentangling the distinct outcomes and effects of lockdowns from the consequences of ambiguously defined “active shooter drills” is an uphill battle.

titleEn: We paid college students about $5 a night to sleep at least 7 hours – and their grades quickly improved
titleZh: 【education】We paid college students about $5 a night to sleep at least 7 hours – and their grades quickly improved
descriptionEn: Universities and colleges won’t necessarily pay students to sleep. But they can offer other incentives that encourage them to close their eyes earlier.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
Paying college students about US$5 a night to sleep seven hours got them a quarter more nights of adequate sleep – and better grades.

That is what we found in a study we published in July 2026 .

We gave more than 1,100 undergraduates at University of Pittsburgh a Fitbit – a wearable activity tracker that looks similar to a watch – and an app that sent bedtime reminders and morning feedback. We randomly chose 468 students and paid them about $5 for every night they slept at least seven hours, over the course of four weeks. We verified how much they slept using the device they wore.

The students were about 19 years old, on average, and half of them were first-year students. Roughly 72% of them were women. About 55% were white, 28% Asian, 9% Black and 4% Hispanic.

Our study shows that offering an immediate financial reward can help students meet a seven-hour sleep goal, and that those effects can persist up to a month beyond when the students are paid.

About one-third of American adults sleep less than seven hours a night, and a similar share say they wish they slept more. Among adolescents and young adults, roughly two-thirds routinely fall short of getting seven hours of sleep a night – the amount of shut-eye that health authorities recommend .

One prominent sleep researcher has called sleep deprivation the most prevalent high-risk behavior.

Short sleep is linked to obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke and early death .

Irregular sleep predicts mortality risk even more than sleep duration does . Sleep loss shows up in decision-making, even when it comes to issues like whether people vote .

Before we changed anything, the average student in our study slept 6.6 hours a night .

Half were going to bed after 1 a.m. on average – a quarter after 2 a.m.

Students got the recommended seven hours of sleep on a typical weeknight on only 43% of their nights, and more than 85% fell short at least once a week.

They also did not know how much sleep they were getting. Two-thirds told us they usually slept seven hours – the trackers showed only about one-third of students slept that much on even three nights out of five.

And 94% said their ideal night of sleep was longer than the one they were getting.

The 468 students we offered nightly payments reached seven hours of sleep on 26% more nights than 380 students who were not offered the money. That is a large shift for a group in which fewer than half were hitting the mark to begin with.

Students receiving the monetary incentive slept 19 more minutes per school night, roughly the difference between closing the laptop at 11:40 p.m. or at midnight.

Among students receiving the payment incentive, their GPA rose by about 0.08 points that semester – roughly a quarter of the gap between students who arrived with above-average and below-average high school grades.

Once the payments stopped after four weeks, students who had received the money were still sleeping about eight minutes longer per night for the remaining three to four weeks of the study. The effect was smaller than during our study, but our findings suggest that some of the change in sleep habits persisted for up to a month after the end of the incentive.

The effects of the intervention on sleep and GPA were largest among first-term freshmen, whose routines are not yet necessarily fixed.

Timing mattered too: Delivering the payment as a lump sum at the end of the semester, rather than every morning, produced only about two-thirds of the effect on sleep.

The effects of the intervention on GPA faded over a couple of academic terms. Grades remained higher in the following semester, but two semesters later we could no longer detect an effect.

Bedtime reminders and morning feedback on their own – with no money attached – had little effect. Students who received them slept only marginally more. The problem was not motivation: Nearly all said they wanted more sleep than they were getting. The challenge was following through on that intention night after night.

Our results show that universities should look at how the environment they create fosters or discourages good sleep habits.

Late evening deadlines to submit assignments and early classes can both make it harder for students to get enough sleep. Changing some of these features costs little compared with many academic support programs, and it may be worth testing alongside other interventions aimed directly at students.

Reminders and feedback might also work better if they change over time, rather than becoming familiar and easy to tune out.

Very few universities or students treat sleep as part of an investment in education, or ask whether the schedules and incentives schools create make adequate sleep harder. Our results suggest they should.

titleEn: School choice proponents say it offers families more options – but those don’t always extend to immigrant students
titleZh: 【education】School choice proponents say it offers families more options – but those don’t always extend to immigrant students
descriptionEn: School choice heavily influences immigrant students’ experiences in Charleston schools and can leave them in segregated academic environments, new findings show.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
Educators , politicians and education observers have long debated school choice.

This controversial policy approach lets families pick alternatives to their assigned neighborhood public schools and, in some cases, allows them to use government funds to pay for private school tuition or other educational expenses.

Some of the school choice debate has focused on whether charter schools – meaning publicly funded, independently operated schools – offer students more equitable educational opportunities and better academic outcomes than traditional public schools.

Not much of the debate has focused on how school choice can affect immigrant students.

We are scholars of social studies education and educational foundations .

In our forthcoming research , we examined the impact of school choice on the academic outcomes of immigrant students, primarily from low-income families.

We found that school choice often leaves them behind, as they struggle to succeed academically in often less-than-ideal educational environments.

From 2024 through 2025, we analyzed the impact that school choice is having on immigrant students in our city, Charleston, South Carolina.

Though South Carolina’s foreign-born population is smaller than it is in some states, it has increased by more than 900% since 1980.

Approximately 7.2% of the residents in Charleston County are foreign-born .

School choice and the rise of charter and magnet schools can heavily influence immigrant students’ experiences in Charleston schools.

As in many parts of the country, charter schools have expanded across Charleston since 1996, when lawmakers first allowed them in the state .

In 2025, South Carolina passed a bill that allows many state residents to use virtual vouchers – or, as they are also called, educational scholarship funds – that people use to pay for scholarships at private schools or, in some cases, to cover home-schooling expenses .

Charter schools have increased inequality and racial and socioeconomic inequality within school systems, some research shows.

In our opinion, this new voucher plan will likely exacerbate these issues.

Another challenge in Charleston is the rise of magnet schools.

Magnet schools are free, public schools that are often specialized in their scope, and they admit students from a range of neighborhoods.

Magnets, similar to charter schools, can be completely separate schools with their own buildings, or housed within a particular section of a traditional public school.

Unlike charter schools, magnet schools often, but not always, determine prospective students’ acceptance based on certain academic criteria, including how well they score on standardized testing and the student’s GPA . Other magnet schools select students based on a lottery.

Magnet schools, whether at the elementary, middle or high school level, tend to attract students from wealthier homes and draw particularly white populations.

One reason is that admission to magnet schools – including Academic Magnet High School , Charleston County’s top public high school – is typically based on test scores.

It is often more difficult for students from low-income families, including some immigrant students, to score well on the tests and qualify for these schools.

Since high-performing magnet schools tend to enroll the most privileged students and experienced staff, other nearby public schools might experience drawbacks, like decreased enrollment and more staff turnover .

Just about a mile from Academic Magnet is North Charleston High School, a traditional public high school that is required to enroll any local resident.

The school has about 830 students , a number smaller than are actually zoned for the school. It also has some of the highest rates of poverty and lowest test scores in the state.

Many students in the area instead attend charter schools , magnet schools or even other traditional public schools that perform better academically , which these students can often attend – if they have their own transportation.

This dynamic often creates various challenges for students who remain at struggling neighborhood schools. These issues include worse student academic performance , reduced teacher retention and increased racial and socioeconomic segregation .

In our forthcoming study, we examined the academic performance and demographics of three Charleston area schools: North Charleston , Academic Magnet and Fort Dorchester , a neighborhood public high school.

Approximately 92.5% of the students at North Charleston are Black or Hispanic.

About half the students at Fort Dorchester are Black or Hispanic.

Meanwhile, only 8.9% of the students at Academic Magnet are Black or Hispanic.

Approximately 100% of the students at North Charleston are economically disadvantaged, meaning they qualify for free or reduced lunch . This compares with 60% of students at Fort Dorchester and 13% at Academic Magnet.

While 39.7% of the teachers at North Charleston left after three years , 18.6% of teachers left during this time frame at Fort Dorchester, and another 13.8% at Academic Magnet.

We wanted to examine how these schools’ academic and demographic differences affect immigrant students and their academic performance.

We found that English language proficiency among non-native English-speaking students at North Charleston was 3.4%. Overall, approximately 9.3% of students there had a level 4 or higher English language score, out of a total six possible points.

At Fort Dorchester, the numbers were much higher: 16.9% of non-native students were proficient in English, and and overall, 34.4% were at level 4 or above in English.

At Academic Magnet, due to the lack of non-native English speakers, no data was available.

We also interviewed some of the teachers in the “left behind” schools like North Charleston in the district. One shared that immigrant students or children of immigrants started having issues, like skipping school or engaging in disruptive behavior, that they saw other kids doing in these schools.

As one teacher said: “I try to get them to understand, this is not all America … I would just feel so bad for that.”

We believe that school choice discussions should include immigrant students and magnet schools. In the often-tense discussions on school choice, public school advocates often see magnet schools in a positive light .

However, our study indicates that school choice can often lead to greater segregation and inequality. School choice proponents often laud the benefits of those who use it, but they rarely discuss those who are left behind.

titleEn: Here’s how teachers and parents can collaborate and help Michigan’s 1.4M students succeed
titleZh: 【education】Here’s how teachers and parents can collaborate and help Michigan’s 1.4M students succeed
descriptionEn: Inflexible meeting times, transportation and childcare challenges can limit parents or caregivers from getting involved in their children’s education.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
About 1.4 million Michigan students returned to the state’s K-12 public school classrooms this fall.

One of the most powerful influences on how these students will perform exists outside the classroom: the quality of the partnerships that schools and families establish with each other.

Establishing these partnerships may be easier than it sounds. Throughout more than four decades as an educator and researcher studying literacy and family engagement , I have learned that most families deeply care about their children’s education and want to work with teachers toward the best possible outcomes.

This message is especially timely in Michigan. Many students continue to experience challenges in reading following the COVID-19 pandemic. Only 39% of Michigan third graders scored proficient or advanced in English language arts on the M-STEP, an annual state exam, in the 2024-25 school year.

In 2024, Michigan students scored below the national average in reading on the National Assessment of Educational Progress . Michigan fourth graders averaged 209 , five points below the national average, while eighth graders averaged 255, compared with 257 nationally.

Although standardized test scores do not fully capture the breadth of students’ knowledge , abilities or potential, they can provide one useful indicator of how well students are developing literacy skills.

National studies also demonstrate that families want to play active roles in their children’s education. They show, too, that many parents seek clearer communication and more meaningful opportunities to collaborate with educators.

In my assessment, one of the most encouraging developments in family engagement research over the past two decades has been the growing recognition among researchers, educators and schools that parents are not simply volunteers who occasionally assist schools. They are co-educators whose knowledge, cultural wealth and lived experiences enrich children’s educational opportunities.

This understanding reflects a broader movement toward educational equity and shared responsibility for student success.

Families may be invited to attend conferences, literacy nights or workshops, but they are not always invited to share their knowledge or participate as equal partners in decisions about their children’s learning.

In my experience, families may feel that educators do not understand their cultural and linguistic practices. They may notice that communication flows primarily from school to home rather than in both directions, or that their knowledge of their own children is undervalued.

For families whose previous encounters with schools have involved judgment, exclusion or racism, or educators focusing on perceived shortcomings rather than recognizing families’ strengths, an invitation to participate does not automatically create understanding.

Some of my most formative lessons came during my early work with African American families in Louisiana. I began spending time with parents and listening carefully to what they understood schools were asking them to do at home.

Teachers frequently encouraged parents to “read to your child,” without explaining what meaningful reading might look like.

Some parents were uncertain about teachers’ expectations or viewed reading primarily as getting the words right. These experiences helped inspire Parents as Partners in Reading , a program I designed to help families support children’s literacy through interactive read-alouds that encourage conversation and making connections between books and children’s everyday lives.

In Louisiana, I showed rather than simply told them how they might make reading with their children more interactive and enjoyable. I modeled how to sit comfortably with a child, let the child hold the book and turn the pages, vary their voices, pause to ask questions, talk together about the pictures and follow the child’s interests and reactions.

Rather than prescribing a single “right” way to read together, these interactions gave parents opportunities to try different approaches, ask questions and discover what worked best for them and their children.

Parents then practiced these approaches with one another before using them. As their confidence increased, the interactions began to flow more naturally: Parents relied less on the strategies I had modeled and became more comfortable following their children’s lead, responding to their questions and comments and allowing conversations about the story to develop spontaneously.

I’ve watched educators transform their relationships with families once they begin viewing parents through their strengths rather than perceived flaws. Families know dimensions of their children that may never be visible during the school day: the child who loves to tell stories at the dinner table, or the child who is fascinated by cars or animals.

When educators listen to those stories, they gain information that can change how they understand and teach a child. Family engagement must also mean creating opportunities for educators to learn from families.

Instead of asking why families are not involved, they begin asking how schools can become more welcoming , more responsive and more collaborative. That shift in perspective often changes the entire culture of a school.

Here are a few ways educators can build relationships with families and vice versa:

Teachers shouldn’t wait until there is a problem to reach out to families. Relationships are strongest when schools communicate with families before challenges arise.

A welcoming phone call, a quick note celebrating something a child did well, an invitation to visit the classroom, or simply taking time to learn about a child’s interests can go a long way.

Parents can make a point of introducing themselves to their child’s teacher early in the school year. Parents might share something the teacher would find helpful to know about their child – what excites them, what they enjoy reading or doing at home, or what helps them feel confident as learners.

These early exchanges also communicate an important message: “I know my child in ways that can help you teach them, and I want us to work together.”

Families should hear from educators, but educators also need to hear from families. Communication is most meaningful when educators listen as much as they inform.

Educators can ask parents and caregivers: What are your hopes for your child this year? What should I know about your child that will help me be a better teacher? How does your child learn best? What is the easiest way for us to stay in touch?

Parents can ask teachers: “What are you noticing about my child as a reader and learner?” and “What are some things we can do at home that would reinforce what you are teaching at school?”

At some point, educators may need to talk with families about academic, behavioral or attendance concerns. Teachers can begin by sharing what the child does well and listening to what the family is seeing at home. Then invite their insights and perspectives: “Here is what I’m noticing. What are you seeing, and how can we work together?” This small shift – from presenting families with a problem to inviting them into a conversation – can transform a potentially difficult exchange into an opportunity for genuine partnership.

Families can listen carefully when teachers raise concerns and ask questions to better understand what the teacher is observing about their child. They can also share what they notice about their child at home, since children may demonstrate different strengths, behaviors and abilities in different settings.

Together, families and teachers can identify strategies to try at home and at school to address the concern and agree on a time to reconnect and discuss the child’s progress.

titleEn: Noise pollution is a serious but often forgotten public health problem
titleZh: 【health】Noise pollution is a serious but often forgotten public health problem
descriptionEn: Creating a quieter environment can improve your health – but you have to know what you’re listening for.
descriptionZh: 此文為即時爬取的英文新聞，建議搭配 AI 摘要功能深入學習。
fullContentEn:
The human body is remarkably good at getting used to the environment around it. You’ve probably experienced this if you’ve ever gone to a matinee and emerged from the dark theater into sunshine. Your eyes sting, so you squint and shield your face until they adjust to the bright sunlight.
